# Transfer Factors: Which Exercise Classes Act on Which, Within One Exercise and Within Whole Motor Actions

**What it is — corrected from a NO-GO review finding.** The prior version of this entry
asserted an ordered "chain" running only general to competitive, with specialized-
developmental and competitive exercises as "the only exercise classes with a direct claim
on transferring to the competitive result." The source does not support that direction-only,
SDE/CE-only reading. Bondarchuk names three factors under study, and the reverse-direction
question in the same breath:

"First is the influence of general developmental exercises on specialized-preparatory,
specialized-developmental, or competitive exercises. Second, is the effect of
specialized-preparatory exercises on specialized-developmental and competitive exercises.
Third are training questions on the effect of specialized-developmental exercises on the
competitive event." He immediately adds the reverse question: "it is necessary to know
how the general-preparatory, specialized-preparatory and specialized-developmental
exercises have an effect on the competitive exercise and **which form of the latter
exercises has an influence on the general-preparatory, specialized-preparatory and
specialized-developmental exercises**." (PDF p. 33, printed p. 16.) So general-preparatory
exercises acting directly on the competitive exercise, and the reverse (competitive-class
exercises influencing the more general classes), are both factors he names as under study,
not ruled out.

He also describes transfer "within the limits of one exercise": training the leg extensor
muscles at one joint angle has a positive effect on strength in other joint angles [95];
similar effects appear using the bench press and varying body angle; training throwers
with the entire throw simultaneously increases results throwing from a standing position;
and "in training long jumpers, when using jumps with a full or short run up, there is a
positive effect on the development of speed in the 30 or 60 meter run" — the run-up length
and the sprint segment, not one run-up length transferring to another. Separately, a
standard-weight implement throw "can have a positive or negative influence on results when
throwing a lighter or heavier weight (implement)" — i.e. this transfer within an exercise
family can run either direction, positive or negative. (PDF p. 33, printed p. 16.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism here. **Inference:** exercises sharing
more of the competitive event's biomechanics, muscle groups, or coordination structure
(see the specifist position in [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]] and
the classification in [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]]) would be expected
to influence each other more reliably, in either direction, than exercises sharing less —
this is this entry's own reading, not something the passage states.

**When to apply** — Use this as the reasoning behind checking both directions of an
exercise-selection audit: not just "does general-preparatory work feed the competitive
exercise" but "does the competitive-class exercise (or a specialized-developmental variant
of it) itself carry information back to how general or specialized-preparatory exercises
should be dosed." **Inference:** Chapter 2 gives two boundary conditions worth reading
alongside this factor list, though the author does not connect them to it in these terms
himself: specialized-preparatory exercises transfer to the competitive result only "up to
a specific level of sports mastery" (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158; see
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] and
[[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]), and general-preparation means build a
"base, foundation" for the competitive event only in low-level athletes, refs [57, 266]
(PDF p. 64, printed p. 47; see also PDF p. 23, printed p. 6, refs [34, 57, 182]).

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is Bondarchuk's own descriptive
model built from the same single dataset referenced throughout the book, not an
independently tested causal chain. **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and
field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic
cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed
p. 59); not football, not team sport. It describes track and field individual events; a
football position group's skill (e.g., pass protection) is a much more complex,
multi-factor competitive action than a single-event track result, so re-applying these
factors to a football skill is Inference, reasonable by analogy but untested here.

**Example** — **Inference:** in sprinting, general conditioning (GPE) may feed hill sprints
or resisted sprints. Resisted sprints repeat the actual sprinting action against added
load, so by the Glossary definition they are specialized-developmental (SDE), not
specialized-preparatory (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii) — not the SPE example this entry
previously used. Flying-start segments or overspeed towing (also SDE) would then feed the
competitive 100m/40-yard result (CE). This chain of examples is this entry's own
construction, not the author's; the author's own within-exercise examples are the joint-
angle, throw-position, and jump-run-up cases given above.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification these
factors operate on. [[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]] —
Chapter 2's empirical test of which specific exercises actually transfer most for
sprinters.

=== PDF 033
Transfer Factors 
 
The theory of training transfer oversees the study of many carry-over factors, beginning 
with the interaction between separate exercises and physical abilities to their mutual 
influence in simple or complex movements.  We will address some of these basic carry-
over factors.  Foremost is the transfer of physical abilities and motor skills when using 
different, according to form and content, means of training.  First is the influence of 
general developmental exercises on specialized-preparatory, specialized-developmental, 
or competitive exercises.  Second, is the effect of specialized-preparatory exercises on 
specialized-developmental and competitive exercises.  Third are training questions on the 
effect of specialized-developmental exercises on the competitive event.   
 
Thus it is necessary to know how the general-preparatory, specialized-preparatory and 
specialized-developmental exercises have an effect on the competitive exercise and 
which form of the latter exercises has an influence on the general-preparatory, 
specialized-preparatory and specialized-developmental exercises. 
 
The transfer of training, within the limits of one exercise, is basically the same when 
using simple or complex (according to their coordinational structure) exercises.  For 
example, training the leg extensor muscles at one joint angle has a positive effect on 
strength in other joint angles [95].  We come up with similar effects in the process of 
using the bench press, the angle of the body and others.  In the training of throwers, when 
using the entire throw, we simultaneously get an increase in sports results when throwing 
from place.  In training long jumpers, when using jumps with a full or short run up, there 
is a positive effect on the development of speed in the 30 or 60 meter run. 
 
Throwing, as for example the standard weight in any track and field throw event, can 
have a positive or negative influence on results when throwing a lighter or heavier weight 
(implement).   
 
16 
=== PDF 035
The Mechanisms of Training Transfer 
 
In dealing with construction of sports form development cycles, specialists are in 
agreement that the level of physical, technical, psychological and other abilities, as well 
as definite functional results in each of the previous stages, the training block, should 
create the “base”, “foundation” for increasing sports achievements in the following 
exercises to be used.  However, none of the specialists make note of when and how the

development.

use of an effective system of exercises for the duration of the following stages, blocks is

previous stage, block, takes place at the beginning of each following stage, block.  In this

=== PDF 039
The Dependence of Training Transfer on the Duration 
of Different Stages, Blocks of Sports Form Development 
Cycles 
 
At the present time, after the regularities regarding development, maintenance and lose of 
sports form have been studied, it becomes clear that the duration of the stages, blocks, of 
sports form development cycles, as proposed by various authors, can serve to reveal the 
mechanisms of training transfer, or to create conditions that do not allow for transfer.  In 
the latter instance, we have in mind situations in which the idea of creating the “base”,  
“foundation”, remains only an idea.  The reason for this is that the work carried out in 
each of the previous stages, blocks, does not show an influence on increasing 
achievements in the training used over the duration of each successive stage.   
 
In life the idea is realized only when at the end of each previous stage, block, the athlete 
resolves the tasks put before him that allows him to enter the state of sports form in the 
training that is used for the duration of the work.  For this to happen it is necessary that 
the duration of the stages, blocks, correspond to the duration of the cycles of sports form 
development for each individual athlete.  From the literature it is known that most 
frequently, athletes, after the period of rest (transitional period), enter into the state of 
sports form over 2-3 months.  But there are also athletes whose individual cycles of 
sports form development take 4-7 and even 8 months. 
 
Practically, only when using the same yearly cycles of training with the duration of the 
general preparatory stage on the average, three months, athletes who enter the state of 
sports form in the exercises used over 2-3 months, can realize creation of a “base”, 
“foundation”, for the training used during specialized preparation stage.  When using two 
and three cycles in the yearly cycle of training, the athletes, at the end of the general 
preparation stages, do not have time to enter into full sports form in the exercises used.  
We remind the reader that when using the two cycle schematic of the yearly cycle, the 
22 
=== PDF 040
duration of the second stage of general preparation (the second preparatory period) varies 
from 4-6 weeks, and in the three cycle plan, it is even less—2-3 weeks. 
 
For example, we will look at one of the schematics of constructing the sports form 
development cycle used by a group of sprinters and hurdlers.  This schematic oversees 
the following alternation of stages: 1) development of general endurance—2) 
development of general strength—3) development of speed and speed endurance— and 
4) entry into the state of sports form.  The duration of the first stage is ten days, second, 
15 days, third, 6-8 weeks and the fourth, 2-3 weeks.   
 
Practically, because of such short periods of time (10-15days) it is impossible to resolve, 
the tasks of developing general endurance and general strength.  At the present time, not 
knowing the regularities for shortening the limits of entering into the state of sports form, 
in 10-15 days it is possible to resolve only the task of preparing the body for the 
forthcoming work in the speed and speed endurance development stage.  The stages of 
developing general endurance and general strength should be called “followers” (tag 
alongs) but in no way “developmental”, capable of creating the “base”, “foundation”, for 
the means of training used during the following stage. 
 
Note that when using this construction scheme for the development of sports form cycles, 
the athletes enter into this state at the end of the fourth stage. The reason for this is that 
sports form begins to develop at the beginning of the stage of speed and speed endurance 
development. 
 
Consequently, it is possible to conclude that only when using stages, blocks, stage-
variants and block-variant means of constructing cycles of sports form development, that 
we can in reality, resolve the task of creating a “base” “foundation”, over the duration of 
the first stages, blocks.  Achieved at the end of these stages or blocks, the level of sports 
results can be realized only at the end of the following stages or blocks.   
 
23 
=== PDF 041
The practical discussion here is of the presence of long term transfer of training, that is 
beginning with the duration of the stages of general preparation or blocks of physical 
preparation, we create the “base”, “foundation” and achieve the planned for level of 
sports results in the exercises being used.  Only later do we address the development of 
sports form in the specialized-preparatory, specialized-developmental and competitive 
exercises, believing that it will serve to increase achievement in the specific sports event. 
 
With this logic it follows that an increase in sports results at the moment of entering into 
the state of sports form in the competitive exercise (event) takes place because of the 
level achieved with general preparation means.  Specialized-preparatory, specialized-
developmental and competitive exercises in this case fulfill a secondary role, only for 
entry into the state of sports form.   
 
It is possible to go along with this presentation if the concept of general and specialized 
preparation unity is upheld in the future and if the created “base”, “foundation” during 
each of the previous stages, blocks, shows a positive influence on increasing the level of 
achievement in the training used during the following trainings.  In this case, it can be 
said that the means of general and specialized preparation, or the physical and technical 
preparation exercises, used during the stages of specialized preparation and blocks of 
technical preparation, have a specific relationship to one another.  They have a mutual 
influence on increasing sports results at the moment of entering the state of sports form. 
 
When using other schematics of constructing sports form cycles in which the training 
means are set up for 1-2 or 2-3 weeks, the transfer of training, due to the created “base”, 
“foundation”, cannot be practically realized.  It is possible only when there is a 
succession in the exercises used over the entire cycle of sports form development that is, 
over the duration of all the cycles, stages, put together in a specific conformity to general 
and specialized preparation means.  The portion of general and specialized exercises can 
change from stage to stage, but they must be used in each of them.  In such cycle 
construction, the athletes can simultaneously enter into the state of sports form in the 
general developmental, specialized-preparatory, specialized-developmental and 
24 
=== PDF 042
competitive exercises.  As a result, there will be a definite level of sports achievement 
attained at the end of the last stage. 
 
We call this view of training transfer, current (flowing), not distant.  It is most frequently 
observed when using the variational, combinational, complex and also some mixed 
means of constructing development of sports form cycles. 
 
Current transfer of training is observed on stages of general preparation and in blocks of 
physical preparation when using the stage and block methods of constructing cycles of 
sports form development.  The exercises used have an effect on one another and serve to 
achieve a definite level of sports results at the end of their use.   
 
Such an understanding of training transfer is also seen when using the complex method of 
constructing cycles of sports form development.  Here, the level of sports form is 
determined by the complex of exercises that are used in the given cycles of sports form 
development. 
 
25 
=== PDF 066
form.  This is current transfer of training. It distinguished from distant transfer by the fact 
that it simplifies transfer since the athlete enters into the sports form state in all of the 
exercises used at the same time.  In distant transfer of training, at the beginning they enter 
into the state of sports form in one form of exercise and only later in others.  In such 
situations, the process of training transfer is made more complex by the fact that the 
athletes must maintain the achieved level of preparation over the duration of each 
following stage, block in certain forms of exercises and at the same time experience 
further development in others.  It is somewhat difficult to do this when organizing the 
training process.   
 
For example, we can look closely at the stage-complex method of constructing cycles of 
sports form development.  Here, the task during the stage of specialized preparation is to 
maintain the achieved level of preparation in the general preparatory exercises and to 
develop sports form in the specialized-preparatory, specialized-developmental and 
competitive exercises. 
 
The regularities of sports form development reveal the essence of the individual limits of 
entering into the given state.  First, the duration of the stages, blocks, during which the 
“base”, “foundation”, is created is made more precise; and second, it is evidence that 
when using the variational method of constructing cycles of sports form development, 
achievement of distant transfer of training from one stage, block, to the following ones, 
cannot be realized because of their short duration.  Here the “base”, “foundation”, over 
the duration of each of the previous stages, blocks, can be created only when the 
succession in the means of training used is maintained.  We have in view here that the 
entire cycle will be used for the general-preparatory, specialized-preparatory, specialized-
developmental and competitive exercises.  But, at the beginning of each stage, block, it is 
necessary to fulfill them according to the schematic, that is, these means are maintained 
but their composition changes periodically. 
 
At the beginning, the proposed division of exercise classification regulates the system of 
exercises employed when using one or another means of constructing cycles of sports 
49 
=== PDF 067
form development.  It likewise makes it possible to understand which forms of exercises 
create the “base” and later on, to which form of exercise it can be transferred to, and by 
so doing, make more precise the mechanisms of physical preparation transfer that are in 
line with the regularities of sports form development. 
 
The proposed system of working out model characteristics makes it possible to search for 
the optimal level of results in the base exercises on each new level of sports 
improvement.   
 
50

36:- The athlete is described as the hub of a wheel, with every support function (academics, Athletic Medicine, nutrition, mental health, Applied Performance) as a spoke — no single discipline owns the athlete's development. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5]
37:- An Athletic Performance coach is framed in explicit contrast to a narrower "Strength Coach" identity: "we/our" and holistic mind-body-spirit development versus "me/my" and just lifting/running. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5; week1-lecture.md p.13]
38:- The current Baylor Applied Performance Operations Guide is judged, by Eric's own gap analysis, as missing: an intern/GA curriculum, sport-specific data dictionaries, daily operational checklists, Baylor-specific (not generic-template) technology workflows, and a guiding-principles/policy framework for staff and interns. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 1, 3.2]
44:- Assessment is continuous, not a single test day: start with movement quality, injury history, and training background, then observe daily via warm-ups and practice. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]
45:- Testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April") or the resulting data cannot be trusted for comparison. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6]
46:- Favor a small number of valid, reliable tests mapped to clear KPI categories over an exhaustive battery — illustrated with a simple baseball profile (bodyweight, 60-yard dash, vertical jump, broad jump, back squat, push-up max). **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6; week1-lecture.md p.16]
47:- Weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early enough to adjust programming. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
48:- Preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation) — both are tracked, but they answer different questions. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
50:- 1RM testing is reserved for intermediate/advanced athletes with real exposure to near-maximal loads; novices and most women's-sport testing default to repetition-max protocols, which are described as better tolerated neurologically, psychologically, and physically for smaller-framed lifters. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.18; week1-lecture.md p.39]
53:- The current data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport, which Eric's own gap analysis flags as a real usability problem for staff and a priority to fix with sport-specific, threshold-contextualized dictionaries. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]
67:- Core GPS metrics tracked: maximum velocity, total distance, player load, field time, heart-rate bands, velocity/acceleration/deceleration effort bands, and Inertial Movement Analysis (IMA) for indoor sessions without GPS coverage. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.11-13, Data Dictionary]
69:- No sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently exist in the documented data dictionary — it is generic and vendor-organized, and building contextualized per-sport thresholds is named as unfinished, prioritized work. **Explicit (gap, stated as a gap)** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]
70:- Heavy GPS/load-monitoring data was described as having bred a "culture of fear" in the field broadly (do less, to protect recovery), which the course material argues actually leaves athletes under-prepared for competition. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10]
78:- Speed is taught as the quality with the shortest ground-contact-time demand (~0.08s male, ~0.10s female at max velocity) and is described as harder to train and more genetically constrained than strength or power, but as the biggest separator between good and great athletes at the elite level. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.11]
82:- The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next) is repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass." **Inferred (transcript + shared course material)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10; week1-lecture.md pp.23,26]
83:- Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of "sport specific." **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16; week1-lecture.md pp.32-36]
84:- The Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky) — matching amplitude/direction of movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production, and regime of muscular work to the sport skill — governs whether an exercise actually transfers, rather than surface resemblance to the sport. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14; week1-lecture.md p.34]
85:- Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13; week1-lecture.md p.31]
86:- Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work. In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule. **Inferred (transcript + shared slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.21]
87:- Undulating/non-linear periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks) is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression, specifically to avoid staleness while still building tolerance for higher loads. **Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed but first-person: "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use")** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-26]
88:- Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment within a training block, used consistently across strength and power teaching. **Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.19; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.15]
89:- Strength's residual training effect is treated as roughly 30 days — a minimal retention dose is still trained within that window, even during lower-strength-emphasis blocks. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-25]
90:- Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21; week1-lecture.md p.46]

118:- Bodyweight-control competency is treated as a marker of injury risk in its own right: an athlete who can bench 400 lb but can't do 10 clean push-ups has "something out of whack" that needs fixing regardless of their strength numbers. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5]
119:- Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]

=== PDF 014
Result 
 
Indice  
Indice usually refers to the number of the recorded result of a 
particular exercise.  It may also refer to results in the exercise, results 
in the competition, etc.  
Specialized  
Exercises  
 
Specialized exercises have a direct correlation to the sports event.  
They have specific criteria and must duplicate various aspects of the 
competitive event, as for example, the biomechanical structure, energy 
source, range of motion in which strength is displayed, etc.  Also 
known as specialized physical preparation (SPP). 
Specialized-
developmental 
exercises 
These exercises repeat the competitive exercise in its separate parts.  
In executing them, one and the same muscle groups participate, 
together with activation of similar systems and organs.  They not only 
repeat the muscle work regime and other systems of the body which 
ensure further increases in the competitive exercise, but also supersede 
them.  The specialized-developmental exercises more or less recreate 
all the elements of the competitive activity, and in so doing, make it 
possible to more effectively and selectively have an effect on 
improving or developing the same or other physical abilities.  The 
levels achieved in these exercises are realized in further execution of 
the competitive exercises.  They serve for entry into the state of sports 
form.   
Specialized-
preparatory 
exercises 
These exercises as the general preparatory exercises, do not repeat the 
competitive actions as a whole or in their separate parts.  However, 
they use similar muscle groups in their execution.  The training work 
serves to activate the functions and body systems from which an 
increase in sports results in the main movements depend.  Identical or 
close to identical regimes of muscle work and different functions of 
other systems are involved.   
Sports Form 
This term typically refers to when the athlete attains all that is possible 
from the specific training done over a specific period of time.  For 
example, entering sports form after working on a particular exercise

# Energy-System Loads Share Many Cardiorespiratory Indices but Not Time-to-Form: Anaerobic-Lactate Work Shortens Entry to Form in Other Loads — the Book States the Alactate/Aerobic Direction Both Ways

**What it is — corrected from a NO-GO review finding.** The prior version of this entry
claimed "a block of aerobic work may build a genuine base for anaerobic-alactate and
anaerobic-lactate capacity" and titled itself around broad, one-directional aerobic-to-
alactate transfer. The source states close to the opposite for the specific question of
whether aerobic loads help alactate **sports form**, and it also contradicts itself
internally on a related point. Both corrections below.

**1. Aerobic training does not build alactate sports form, and hurts speed.** Right after
counting how many cardiovascular/respiratory **indices** transfer between aerobic and
anaerobic-alactate loads (see the counts below), Bondarchuk states plainly: "The first form
of loads (aerobic) does not show an influence on the development of sports form in the
second form of loads. In other words, in the state of sports form development the aerobic
and anaerobic-alactate abilities of the athlete that come into play are not-dependent on
one another (our data)... aerobic work shows negatively on the development of speed
capabilities." (PDF p. 163, printed p. 146, opened as an image to confirm the text layer.)
So the index-transfer counts below describe shared cardiorespiratory adaptation, not
transfer of competitive sports form, which the author explicitly denies for this pair.

**2. Internal contradiction on which load shortens time-to-form between aerobic and
anaerobic-alactate — kept visible per the brief, not harmonized, `confidence: contested`.**
Three passages give different answers:
- PDF p. 164, printed p. 147 (discussing Table 106, anaerobic-alactate → anaerobic-lactate):
  "The anaerobic-alactate training loads do not influence the time of entering the state of
  sports form in anaerobic-lactate. At the same time the latter (anaerobic-lactate) shorten
  the amount of time for entering into the given state in the first form of loads
  (anaerobic-alactate)." This passage is about alactate/lactate, not aerobic/alactate.
- PDF p. 165, printed p. 148 (closing the aerobic/anaerobic-lactate discussion, table 109):
  "Anaerobic-alactate training loads shorten the amount of time of entering into a state of
  sports form in the aerobic exercises. At this time the latter appear to be inert in
  comparison to the first."
- PDF p. 173, printed p. 156: "It was found that anaerobic-lactate loads shorten the time
  for entering into the sports form state in aerobic and anaerobic-alactate. At this time,
  the latter do not influence (do not shorten) the amount of time taken to enter the given
  state in the anaerobic-lactate training loads."
PDF p. 165 says **anaerobic-alactate** shortens aerobic's time-to-form; PDF p. 173 says it
is **anaerobic-lactate** that shortens both aerobic's and anaerobic-alactate's time-to-form.
These cannot both be the full picture. Do not resolve this silently; treat both statements
as the book's own record and cite both locators whenever citing either.

**Index-transfer counts (cardiorespiratory and related indices, not sports-form transfer):**
- **Aerobic → anaerobic-alactate**: "6 of 7" cardiovascular/respiratory functional indices
  are "fully transferable" (Table 104, PDF p. 162, printed p. 145). Non-transferable:
  blood-lactate level and most energy-formation/energy-source factors, consistent with
  different fiber-type recruitment (red/slow fibers in aerobic work vs. white/fast fibers
  in anaerobic-alactate work, per the table's own row).
- **Aerobic ↔ anaerobic-lactate**: "of the 16 tests looked at, only four were
  non-transferable" (Table 105, PDF p. 163, printed p. 146).
- **Anaerobic-alactate → aerobic**: "non-transferable factors here are all the remaining
  factors — 13 out of 15" (Table 108, PDF p. 164, printed p. 147), attributed to the
  oxygen-deficient conditions anaerobic-alactate work requires versus the oxygen-dependent
  structure of aerobic work.
- **Anaerobic-lactate → anaerobic-alactate**: Table 107's data show the anaerobic-lactate
  loads "bring about much greater functional shifts in the corresponding body systems than
  the anaerobic-alactate, even though the same (white) muscle fibers participate," and "the
  first form of work [anaerobic-lactate] shortens the time period for entering into the
  state of sports form in the second form of loads [anaerobic-alactate]" — the author adds
  "It is not known why." (Table 107, PDF p. 164, printed p. 147.) This is a one-way
  shortening effect (lactate → alactate), not a "also limited" finding.
- Table 106's own printed title reads "Aerobic-Alactate... to the Aerobic-Lactate" (PDF
  p. 168, printed p. 151) — a source typo to note, not a transcription error in this entry.

Bondarchuk names a single-athlete example of well-combined aerobic/anaerobic training:
"S. Auita" (**Inference:** almost certainly Saïd Aouita, transliterated) held world records
simultaneously across the 1500m, 5000m, and 2-mile distances, was within tenths of a
second of record pace at 2000m/3000m/1 mile, and is listed with additional career bests:
200m-22.8, 400m-46.9, 1000m-2:15.16, steeplechase-8:21.92, 10,000m-27:26.11. (PDF p. 172,
printed p. 155.)

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own stated explanation for the index-transfer pattern is
fiber-type recruitment: aerobic training loads primarily adapt red (slow-twitch) fibers,
while anaerobic-alactate and anaerobic-lactate loads primarily adapt white (fast-twitch)
fibers. He states plainly for the alactate→alactate asymmetry that "it is not known why"
one direction shortens time-to-sports-form and the other does not (PDF p. 164, printed
p. 147) — the author himself flags this as an open question. No mechanism is given for the
aerobic/anaerobic-alactate sports-form independence in point 1 above, or for the internal
contradiction in point 2. Do not read a fuller physiological explanation into this than the
fiber-type note the text actually gives.

**When to apply** — Use this entry as a caution against assuming energy-system training
transfers to competitive sports form the way shared physiological indices might suggest.
Bondarchuk's own data: aerobic loads did not influence anaerobic-alactate sports form, and
aerobic work hurt speed development (PDF p. 163, printed p. 146). Do not use this entry to
support "a block of aerobic work builds a base for alactate capacity" — the author states
the opposite for sports-form transfer specifically, even though many cardiorespiratory
indices are shared. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 already teaches that all three energy
systems are always active simultaneously and that programming should target the intended
adaptation rather than the drill label (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `week3-lecture.md p.19`; `class-4-2026.md p.15`). **Inference:** this
entry's asymmetry and contradiction findings complicate any simple version of that general
principle for the aerobic/alactate pair specifically.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is contested**: the source itself states the direction
of the aerobic/anaerobic-alactate/anaerobic-lactate time-to-form relationship differently
at PDF p. 165 (printed p. 148) versus PDF p. 173 (printed p. 156); see point 2 above. Do
not silently pick one side. **Confidence is untested for the S. Auita/Aouita example**, a
single named-athlete case offered as illustration, not independent evidence. **Population:**
native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly
from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8,
printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport — no football or
team-sport population appears anywhere in this book. The specific physiological index
values (e.g. lactic acid concentrations, VO2 figures) are dataset-specific and should not
be treated as current normative standards.

**Example** — **Inference:** a program that substitutes heavy sprint/power
("anaerobic-alactate") conditioning for aerobic base work, expecting it to also build
aerobic capacity, is not supported by this data: per Table 108, 13 of 15 tracked indices
showed no transfer in that direction. The reverse claim — that aerobic work builds a base
for anaerobic-alactate sports form — is directly contradicted by the author's own PDF
p. 163 statement (point 1 above), even though the shared-index count (Table 104) might
suggest otherwise; do not conflate index overlap with sports-form transfer.

**Related** — No existing library entry addresses this specific aerobic/anaerobic transfer
asymmetry; cross-reference with `method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems,"
for Eric's own energy-system programming framework, and with
[[claim--endurance-event-transfer-range-widens-with-distance]] for the companion finding
on how far training segment distances (rather than energy-system type) transfer within a
single distance-running event.

Bondarchuk's own data: aerobic loads did not influence anaerobic-alactate sports form, and
aerobic work hurt speed development (PDF p. 163, printed p. 146). Do not use this entry to
support "a block of aerobic work builds a base for alactate capacity" — the author states
the opposite for sports-form transfer specifically, even though many cardiorespiratory
indices are shared. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 already teaches that all three energy
systems are always active simultaneously and that programming should target the intended
adaptation rather than the drill label (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `week3-lecture.md p.19`; `class-4-2026.md p.15`). **Inference:** this
entry's asymmetry and contradiction findings complicate any simple version of that general
principle for the aerobic/alactate pair specifically.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is contested**: the source itself states the direction
of the aerobic/anaerobic-alactate/anaerobic-lactate time-to-form relationship differently
at PDF p. 165 (printed p. 148) versus PDF p. 173 (printed p. 156); see point 2 above. Do
not silently pick one side. **Confidence is untested for the S. Auita/Aouita example**, a
single named-athlete case offered as illustration, not independent evidence. **Population:**
native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly
from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8,
printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport — no football or
team-sport population appears anywhere in this book. The specific physiological index
values (e.g. lactic acid concentrations, VO2 figures) are dataset-specific and should not
be treated as current normative standards.

**Example** — **Inference:** a program that substitutes heavy sprint/power
("anaerobic-alactate") conditioning for aerobic base work, expecting it to also build
aerobic capacity, is not supported by this data: per Table 108, 13 of 15 tracked indices
showed no transfer in that direction. The reverse claim — that aerobic work builds a base
for anaerobic-alactate sports form — is directly contradicted by the author's own PDF
p. 163 statement (point 1 above), even though the shared-index count (Table 104) might
suggest otherwise; do not conflate index overlap with sports-form transfer.

**Related** — No existing library entry addresses this specific aerobic/anaerobic transfer
asymmetry; cross-reference with `method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems,"
for Eric's own energy-system programming framework, and with
[[claim--endurance-event-transfer-range-widens-with-distance]] for the companion finding
on how far training segment distances (rather than energy-system type) transfer within a
single distance-running event.

=== PDF 162
use means of developing aerobic capabilities and to use them at the beginning of the 
cycles of developing sports form.  The duration of their use as for example, when using 
stages in constructing the periods, usually lasts several months and its variants from 2-4 
weeks.   
 
The specifics of the created “base”, “foundation”, can only be guessed at.  But most often 
it means increasing the functional state, first of all of the cardiovascular, blood vessel and 
respiratory systems.  Also looked at is the formation and energy provision for the aerobic, 
anaerobic-alactate and anaerobic-lactate training loads. Almost nothing is said about the 
achievement of a definite level of sports results in the longer distances in comparison to 
the competitive event. 
 
With sorrow, in the literature sources available to us, we did not see any research studies 
that looked at the influence of anaerobic-alactate and anaerobic-lactate training loads not 
only one on the other, but on the aerobic.  But the fact that they can have a specific 
interaction with each other, as substantiated in a great deal of factual material, can reveal 
the essence of the reactions produced by one or another of these body systems in 
response to only the aerobic, anaerobic-alactate and anaerobic-lactate training loads.   
 
By considering the data available we will try to further reveal all the transferable (fully 
and partially) and non-transferable factors from one form of activity to another.  Besides 
this, we will examine the positive and negative interactions between the aerobic and 
anaerobic training loads.  In our discussions we will compare the most frequently used 
logical biochemical and pedagological tests that use aerobic, anaerobic-alactate and 
anaerobic-lactate training loads. We will then try, from a theoretical standpoint, to 
explain many questions regarding the interaction between them. Especially important in 
this is to show the interaction of factors that can be used in sports practice. 
 
In table 104, data is presented that characterizes the transferred factors from aerobic 
training loads to anaerobic-alactate.  Most of the functional indices that have a 
relationship to the activity of the cardiovascular and respiratory systems (6 of 7), are fully 
145 
=== PDF 163
transferable.  The non-transferable factors include tests that determine the level of lactic 
acid in the blood and likewise most of the energy forming and energy ensuring work 
factors.  In work fulfilling aerobic training loads the red (slow) muscle fibers participate 
while in the anaerobic-alactate—the white (fast) fibers.   
 
The first form of loads (aerobic) does not show an influence on the development of sports 
form in the second form of loads.  In other words, in the state of sports form development 
the aerobic and anaerobic-alactate abilities of the athlete that come into play are not-
dependent on one another (our data).  It is also necessary to note that in the theory and 
methods of physical education, it is known that aerobic training loads act favorably on 
the break up of lactic acid and in other restorative processes.  Aside from this, aerobic 
work shows negatively on the development of speed capabilities. 
 
Several other results were received when determining the inter-influence between aerobic 
and anaerobic-lactate training loads (table 105).  It appears that of the 16 tests looked at, 
only four were non-transferable.  The greatest differences were seen in the content of 
lactic acid after aerobic and anaerobic-lactate training loads.  The anaerobic-lactate 
regime serves the flow of different adaptational processes in the white muscle fibers and 
in the aerobic regime – red fibers. The anaerobic exercises do not have an influence on 
the time of entering into the state of sports form in development of anaerobic-lactate 
capabilities.   
 
However, the anaerobic-lactate training loads shorten the amount of time needed to enter 
sports form in the aerobic exercises.  The aerobic training work serves to break up the 
lactic acid, the content of which reaches 250-300mg per 100ml of blood after anaerobic-
lactate loads. 
 
The anaerobic-alactate training loads, in suppressing most of the test indices, give in to 
the anaerobic-lactate (table 106). We have in view here mainly those tests that study the 
functional state of the heart-circulatory, blood vessel and respiratory systems.  But, they 
also have other energy forming and energy ensuring work factors.  The anaerobic-alactate 
146 
=== PDF 164
training loads do not influence the time of entering the state of sports form in anaerobic-
lactate.  At the same time the latter (anaerobic-lactate) shorten the amount of time for 
entering into the given state in the first form of loads (anaerobic-alactate).  However, in 
using the anaerobic-alactate and anaerobic-lactate training loads, one and the same 
muscle fibers participate –the white. 
 
Presented in table 107, are the transferable factors of the anaerobic-lactate training loads 
to the anaerobic-alactate loads.  The data presented show that the anaerobic-lactate loads 
bring about much greater functional shifts in the corresponding body systems than the 
anaerobic-alactate, even though the same (white) muscle fibers participate in the work.  It 
is not known why, but the first form of work shortens the time period for entering into the 
state of sports form in the second form of loads.  They have different sources of energy 
formation, time of its effect, and likewise the duration of its apportionment.   
 
Anaerobic-alactate and aerobic training loads bring about the same reactions of the heart- 
circulatory system—(CV).  Also coinciding are indices from other tests which 
characterize the functional state of the respiratory system (oxygen debt, maximum 
oxygen uptake (MO2)) that takes place at the level of lactic acid accumulation (table 
108).  Non-transferable factors here are all the remaining factors – 13 out of 15.  The 
presence of such a large number of non-transferable factors can be explained by the fact 
that in using the anaerobic training loads, the body must execute work in oxygen 
deficient conditions.   
 
Aerobic training loads are accompanied with the use of a great amount of oxygen which 
distinguishes them from the anaerobic loads.  In aerobic loads the transport and 
utilization of oxygen is determined by the structure of the body systems.  They have 
different energy formation and energy ensuring work factors.  In using anaerobic-alactate 
training loads we allow for the flow of different adaptational restructurings in the white 
muscle fibers and in the aerobic, red fibers.  The latter factor apparently explains to a 
great extent why these two forms of training do not have an influence on the time of 
entering into a state of sports form.  It is true that when using several means of 
147 
=== PDF 165
constructing cycles of sports form development, the time of their use can coincide or be 
different. 
 
The anaerobic-lactate training loads are more transferable to the aerobic than to the 
anaerobic-alactate (table 109).  In most cases, the functional state of the cardiovascular 
system, blood vessel and respiratory systems, when using the anaerobic-lactate work is 
significantly higher than in aerobic.  The same amounts are seen in the level of oxygen 
utilization in the process of working out.  There are identical indices of maximum oxygen 
utilization.  Because of this, lactic acid content when using anaerobic-lactate training 
loads is several times higher than in cases when using aerobic -- 250-300mg as opposed 
to 80-100mg.  Energy formation and energy ensuring work factors often coincide.   
 
Anaerobic-lactate training work brings about specific adaptational changes in the white 
muscle fibers and aerobic work brings about specific adaptational changes in the red 
fibers.  Anaerobic-alactate training loads shorten the amount of time of entering into a 
state of sports form in the aerobic exercises.  At this time the latter appear to be inert in 
comparison to the first.   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
148

all of them are beyond our desire for some form of interaction between them.  If we agree

constructing cycles of sports form development, then not only does aerobic training work

influence on the first.   
 
The combined use of aerobic, anaerobic-alactate, anaerobic-lactate training loads (we 
have in view situations in which the variational and complex methods of constructing the 
above mentioned cycles are used) will appear in a specific interrelationship and have a 
definite form of action or influence on the development of one or another type of 
endurance.  In some situations the transfer can be positive, in others negative and 
sometimes neutral.  The reaction noted in a given situation depends upon the optimal 
combination of the three forms of training loads.

combination of aerobic and anaerobic means of training, athletes can show high results in 
several distances.  For example, S. Auita more than once set a world record in the 1500m, 
5,000m, and 2 mile runs.  Besides this, tenths of a second differences distinguished him 
from other record achievements in the 2,000m, 3,000m and 1 mile runs.  And here are 
still more results in other events: 200m-22.8 400m-46.9, 1000m-2:15.16, steeple chase-
8:21.92 and 10,000m-27:26.11.

development of sports form after the transitional periods in cyclical sports events.  It was 
found that anaerobic-lactate loads shorten the time for entering into the sports form state

muscle fibers.  It has long been considered that the aerobic training loads serve to change 
the first type of fiber (red) and the anaerobic the second (white). They take up a full 
specter of adaptational restructurings beginning with capillarization and innervations and 
ending with fine changes in the structure of the red and white muscle fibers.

take place in the nerve-muscle system under the influence of aerobic training loads,

a great extent on the methods of constructing the cycles of developing sports form.

# Implement-Weight Variation Works Best Close to Competition Weight, and History Shows an Overdose Is Possible: The "Throwing Boom"

**What it is — new entry, review's Missing Item 4.** This entry gathers three related
facts about how throwers historically dosed lighter/heavier-implement work, none of which
were captured by the correlational-transfer entry
[[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]] even after that entry's own
review fixes.

**1. The dosing law: correlations peak close to competition weight, not far from it.**
"The greatest amounts of correlational interrelationships were most frequently found in
cases where the deviations [from the competitive implement weight] was insignificant in
relation to the competitive — from 10-20%." The weakest values in the whole implement-weight
dataset came from the largest deviations: 0.425 for the 16kg hammer weight at the 60-65m
level, and 0.365 between the 5.0kg and 7.260kg shot at the 20-21m level. (PDF p. 115,
printed p. 98.)

**2. Historical practice and how much training time this now takes.** "It is generally
known that for developing strength abilities, heavier implements are used and for speed,
lighter." For most of the 20th century, throwers used mainly the competitive-weight
implement, with lighter/heavier implements used "sporadically and in small volume" —
heavier implements in the fall-winter season, lighter implements immediately before
competition, typically in 4-6 week cycles. "In the last two decades" (relative to this
book's writing) that changed: lighter, heavier, and competitive-weight implement work
together now comprises **30-50% of the total training time** across the yearly cycle. (PDF
p. 114, printed p. 97.) Distance-difference norms for specific implement/weight pairs by
event and sex are given in Tables 35-40 (PDF pp. 62-64, printed pp. 45-47; see
[[claim--model-characteristic-tables-exist-by-qualification]] for the values).

**3. The "throwing boom" overdose warning.** Bondarchuk names a real historical error, not
a hypothetical one: "the 'throwing' boom which lasted for several Olympic cycles, in which
the athletes in one training session executed from 200-300 or more throws from place using
lighter or heavier implements. My record holders were included in this group. For example,
some hammer throwers executed up to 500 [1] throws of a weight in one training session."
He dates it: "The 'throwing' boom began after the 19th Olympic games in Mexico and ended
before the 22nd Olympic games in Moscow" (i.e., roughly 1968-1980). He states the boom
"produced negative after-effects" and recommends specialists "increase the volume of
training loads of specialized-developmental exercises up to reasonable amounts in order to
avoid the errors made by throwers in past years." Separately, he notes that in sports
practice "many specialists are already convinced that the use of imitational exercises
without resistance[s], do not have a positive influence on the development of physical
abilities of low as well as high level athletes" — i.e. dropping the implement's weight
entirely (miming the throw) is not a safe substitute either; the dosing problem runs in
both directions. (PDF p. 133, printed p. 116.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for why 200-300+ throws per session produced
negative after-effects, or for why the 10-20% weight-deviation band produces the strongest
correlations. **Inference:** both points are consistent with a dose-response reading —
enough load variation to stress the target quality (strength via heavier, speed via
lighter) without drifting so far from the competitive movement's loading that technique or
recovery capacity breaks down — but the author does not state this interpretation himself
in the excerpted text.

**When to apply** — When programming implement-weight variation for a thrower (or
building an analogous variable-resistance protocol for another sport), use this entry as a
historical caution on both dosing axes: (a) keep the weight deviation from competition
implement modest (per the 10-20% band above) rather than assuming "more extreme is
better," and (b) do not assume "more volume of variable-weight throws is always more
transferable" — the throwing-boom history shows a real, named historical case where
volume (200-500 throws/session) produced negative after-effects, not better transfer.
**Inference:** mapped loosely onto a non-throws context, this reads as a general caution
against unbounded volume escalation of any specialized-developmental variant, not just
implement-weight throws — that generalization is this entry's own, not the author's.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** **A positive interrelationship begins
at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); this entry's dosing law describes which correlations
run highest within that already-positive range, not a pass/fail threshold. **Population:**
native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly
from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8,
printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport. The "throwing
boom" is a specific, dated historical episode (roughly 1968-1980) in Soviet-bloc throws
training, not a controlled study; Bondarchuk gives no session count, athlete count, or
comparison-condition data for the "negative after-effects" claim, and he includes his own
record-holding athletes among those who did it, without saying whether or how it affected
their specific results. Applying the 200-300-throw figure as a hard ceiling for a different
sport's variable-resistance work is Inference by analogy, not something this data tests.

**Example** — **Inference:** a hammer throwing program that rotates through implements
7.26kg (competition), 6kg, and 8kg (roughly 10-17% off competition weight) is better
supported by the dosing law above than one that jumps straight to 16kg or a bare-bar
imitation throw; and a coach programming 200+ standing throws in a single session, echoing
the historical "throwing boom," should treat that volume as a documented historical
cautionary case, not a target.

**Related** — [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]] — the
correlational finding this entry's dosing law and overdose warning were missing from.
[[claim--model-characteristic-tables-exist-by-qualification]] — Tables 35-40's specific
distance-difference norms by implement/weight pair. [[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]]
— this book folder's Method paragraph (questionnaires, four Olympic cycles, 0.349
threshold, steroid exclusion), which this entry's dosing-law correlations also fall under.
=== PDF 114
Transfer of Physical Abilities in the Throws with the 
Use of Different Types of Exercises 
 
The core of the training system for throwers appears to be, that over the duration of the 
yearly cycle, the athletes use a sufficiently large number of exercises repeating the basic 
movement in lighter and more difficult conditions --- i.e., using implements having 
different weights.  The deviation range when using lighter and heavier implements in 
comparison to the competitive implement weight, can vary from several percent to the 
tens and even hundreds of percent.   
 
It is generally known that for developing strength abilities, heavier implements are used 
and for speed, lighter.  In the last two decades the total training loads used in the year-
round training cycle with the use of lighter, heavier and competitive weight implements 
varied between 30-50% of the total amount of time used for training.   
 
In the last 50-60 years in the past century, athletes basically used the competitive weight 
implement.  Heavier and lighter implements were used sporadically and in small volume.  
It was thought that heavier implements should be used in the fall-winter season and 
lighter weights-should be included in the training immediately before the beginning of 
competition.  Usually the heavier and lighter implements were used during 4-6 week 
cycles. 
 
Literary sources which touch on the study of this problem [18, 33, 265, 266] testify to the 
positive influence of lighter and heavier implements on an increase in sports 
achievements in the basic throws.  It was correctly noted that heavier implements can 
have a positive influence on an increase in physical abilities and a negative one on 
technical mastery [18, 152]. 
 
The experimental material received by us in the process of evaluating questionnaires 
filled out by athletes having various sports qualifications (see tables 69-84) testify to the 
97 
=== PDF 115
presence of a positive correlational interrelationship between lighter, heavier and 
competitive weight implements in the structure of the entire movement in all types of 
throws, on different levels of sports mastery.  The greatest amounts of correlational 
interrelationships were most frequently found in cases where the deviations between the 
lighter and heavier implement weights was insignificant in relation to the competitive---
from 10-20%.  The smallest correlation was fixed in the hammer throw when athletes had 
results in the at 60-65m range when throwing the 16kg weight (0.425).  A weak 
interrelationship (0.365) was observed between results in the shotput with weights of 5.0 
and 7.260 kg in athletes throwing the shot 20-21m. 
 
The compiled data once again substantiated the correctness of the position in the theory 
and practice of track and field, that throws with lighter and heavier implements appear to 
be the most transferable to the competitive exercise.  The reason for this is that they are 
identical to themselves according to the basic parameters beginning with the technical 
and rhythmical composition and ending with the consecutiveness of inclusion of the 
muscular groups in the execution, the muscle work regimes and so on.   
 
What is pertinent here is that those negative consequences, which always have a place 
here, are so insignificant that after ceasing use of one or another lighter or heavier 
implement, they can be eliminated in several weekly cycles.  The latter of these (heavier 
implements) relates to the deviations in technical mastery which has been noted by 
several authors [18, 152].  Foremost among these is the change in the release angle of the 
implement during the final effort, the deviation or lean of the trunk backward, the 
decreased amplitude of movement of the implement and so on.   
 
In practically all track and field disciplines, there are no identical actions, according to all 
parameters of the exercise, that repeat those in the competitive event.  Because of this, 
when using one or another exercise, it is necessary to a large measure, to think of its 
positive effects, not about its negatives.  The exercises should be selected so that the 
positive influence prevails. 
 
98 
=== PDF 133
 
However, the effect from using them will have a place only in instances where lighter or 
heavier implements are used.  In sports practice, many specialists are already convinced 
that the use of imitational exercises without resistance, do not have a positive influence 
on the development of physical abilities of low as well as high level athletes.   
 
For development of speed-strength abilities of the legs, specialists recommend an 
increase in the volume of training loads of specialized-developmental exercises up to 
reasonable amounts in order to avoid the errors made by throwers in past years.  We have 
in mind the “throwing” boom which lasted for several Olympic cycles, in which the 
athletes in one training session executed from 200-300 or more throws from place using 
lighter or heavier implements.  My record holders were included in this group.   
 
For example, some hammer throwers executed up to 500 [1] throws of a weight in one 
training session.  The “throwing” boom began after the 19th Olympic games in Mexico 
and ended before the 22nd Olympic games in Moscow.  We did not want to witness the 
“imitational” or “turn-skip” booms.  There should be an optimal amount everywhere or 
the after-effect will be fraught with negative consequences. 
 
We will now look at the interrelationship between specialized-preparatory and 
competitive exercises.  We will begin with means of developing strength abilities.  Their 
total sum at the present time comprises from 30-60% of the total amount of time taken in 
training during the cycles of developing sports form.  From a questionnaire given to 
athletes having different sports qualifications, we were able to determine two global 
strength exercises (snatch and power clean) and two local exercises (squat with a barbell 
on the shoulders and bench press).  The exceptions here appear to be hammer throwers, 
for whom we did not consider results in the bench press, as this exercise is not used by 
most of them in the process of training. 
 
In the discus throw a positive correlational interrelationship between indices in the snatch 
and throws of the competitive implement was observed on the level of 45-50m in men 
116

---

# The Book's Four Exercise Classes, from Its Own Glossary: General Preparatory, Specialized-Preparatory, Specialized-Developmental, Competitive

**What it is** — This is the book's own definition of the classification Chapter 2's
correlational data depends on, drawn from its front-matter Glossary (PDF pp. 10-14,
printed pp. ix-xiii; Chapter 2's own prose, PDF p. 75, printed p. 58, assumes the reader
already knows these terms and does not redefine them). **Voice note:** the Glossary is
unsigned and contains lines in the translator's voice: "In the U.S., these terms are most
often used interchangeably" (Means and Methods entry) and "The physical education
discipline is more highly developed and scientific in the Russian literature than in the
U.S." (Physical Education entry), plus "This is a unique term that has no analogy in the
English language" (Motor Analyzer entry) — all PDF p. 13, printed p. xii. Per the task
brief's rule, a translator (Yessis) voice is not the author's. Treat the definitions below as
**the translated edition's**, possibly Yessis's own glosses; Bondarchuk's own usage of these
terms is visible in Chapter 1-2 prose instead (e.g. PDF p. 24, printed p. 7; PDF p. 62,
printed p. 45, "we did not take exercises from the general developmental group"). Do not
cite this entry as "Bondarchuk says" in a future entry without that caveat. The Glossary's
own abbreviation is "SPP" for **Specialized Exercises** ("Also known as specialized
physical preparation (SPP)," PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii) — a different label than
"specialized-preparatory," which the Glossary does not itself abbreviate. The Glossary
never abbreviates specialized-developmental exercises or competitive exercises as "SDE" or
"CE" either; those abbreviations below are this entry's own shorthand, not the book's:
- **General (Preparatory) Exercises ("GPP" — this entry's abbreviation)**: "do not repeat
  the competitive actions as a whole or their separate parts. Other muscle groups take part
  in the work being done. The functional systems of the body are activated but do not
  ensure an increase in results in the competitive exercise." Function: all-round
  development, work capacity, and active rest/restoration. (PDF p. 12, printed p. xi.)
- **Specialized-Preparatory Exercises ("SPE" — this entry's abbreviation; the Glossary's own
  "SPP" label attaches to a related but separately defined "Specialized Exercises" entry,
  see above)**: like general exercises, "do not repeat the competitive actions as a whole
  or in their separate parts. However, they use similar muscle groups in their execution,"
  activating the functions and body systems the main movement depends on, with "identical
  or close to identical regimes of muscle work." (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Specialized-Developmental Exercises ("SDE" — this entry's abbreviation, not the
  Glossary's)**: "repeat the competitive exercise in its separate parts. In executing them,
  one and the same muscle groups participate, together with activation of similar systems
  and organs. They not only repeat the muscle work regime and other systems of the
  body... but also supersede them," and "serve for entry into the state of sports form."
  (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Competitive Exercises ("CE" — this entry's abbreviation, not the Glossary's)**: "the
  acting definition... is 'sport event,' in which the athlete participates in competition,"
  executed either in actual competition or in training as a model/repeat of competitive
  conditions, easier or harder (this definition spans a page break). (PDF pp. 11-12, printed
  pp. x-xi.)
Chapter 2's own intro adds a cross-cutting distinction independent of the four classes: a
**local** exercise (uses separate parts/body links — squat, bench press, standing long
jump, vertical jump) versus a **global** exercise (uses all body links together — the
barbell clean). (PDF p. 75, printed p. 58.)

**Why it works** — The Glossary gives no stated mechanism for why these four classes
should differ in transfer value; it only defines them by how much of the competitive
movement each one reproduces. **Inference:** reading the four classes as an ordered
continuum, and connecting that continuum to
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] and the specifist "identical
elements" position in [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]] (more shared
elements with the competitive movement predicting more reliable transfer), is this entry's
own synthesis across sections of the book, not a claim the Glossary or Chapter 2's intro
states in those words. Chapter 2's correlational data (see the claim entries below) can be
read as an empirical test of that inferred prediction, event by event, but the book itself
does not frame its own tables that way.

**When to apply** — Use as the primary-source definition when auditing any exercise
selection against this taxonomy, in place of or alongside secondary paraphrases of it.
**Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in HHPR 5355 is taught "on a spectrum from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of 'sport specific'"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`; `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`) — this entry
gives that course material its primary-source citation and exact definitions. This
library already has a secondary-source treatment of the same taxonomy in
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault), built from Moyer's course paraphrase rather than Bondarchuk's own text; that
entry's table ("GPE/SPE/SDE/CE") matches this one closely but labels Moyer's own sprint
examples (bounding, banded pawback, etc.), not Bondarchuk's.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported**, not proven: this is the book's own
classification scheme (see the voice note above on Glossary authorship). Two other sources
in this library already use it independently
(the `fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer` vault entry linked above, and Eric's HHPR 5355
course per `method-baseline.md`), which is evidence the taxonomy circulated beyond this
one book, but this ingest did not check how far it spread through the wider Soviet/Russian
sport-science literature, so that broader claim is not made here. It is a practitioner
taxonomy, not an independently tested causal model, and the boundary between
classes is fuzzy in application (the Moyer-derived entry below makes the same point about
sprint exercises specifically). **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and field
athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles
plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not
football, not team sport. The four-class definitions here are written for individual
track and field events; a football skill (e.g., a pass rush) is a much less discrete,
single "competitive exercise" than a 100m sprint or a hammer throw, so classifying a given
drill as SPE vs. SDE for football is Inference, not something the Glossary addresses.

# The Book's Four Exercise Classes, from Its Own Glossary: General Preparatory, Specialized-Preparatory, Specialized-Developmental, Competitive

**What it is** — This is the book's own definition of the classification Chapter 2's
correlational data depends on, drawn from its front-matter Glossary (PDF pp. 10-14,
printed pp. ix-xiii; Chapter 2's own prose, PDF p. 75, printed p. 58, assumes the reader
already knows these terms and does not redefine them). **Voice note:** the Glossary is
unsigned and contains lines in the translator's voice: "In the U.S., these terms are most
often used interchangeably" (Means and Methods entry) and "The physical education
discipline is more highly developed and scientific in the Russian literature than in the
U.S." (Physical Education entry), plus "This is a unique term that has no analogy in the
English language" (Motor Analyzer entry) — all PDF p. 13, printed p. xii. Per the task
brief's rule, a translator (Yessis) voice is not the author's. Treat the definitions below as
**the translated edition's**, possibly Yessis's own glosses; Bondarchuk's own usage of these
terms is visible in Chapter 1-2 prose instead (e.g. PDF p. 24, printed p. 7; PDF p. 62,
printed p. 45, "we did not take exercises from the general developmental group"). Do not
cite this entry as "Bondarchuk says" in a future entry without that caveat. The Glossary's
own abbreviation is "SPP" for **Specialized Exercises** ("Also known as specialized
physical preparation (SPP)," PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii) — a different label than
"specialized-preparatory," which the Glossary does not itself abbreviate. The Glossary
never abbreviates specialized-developmental exercises or competitive exercises as "SDE" or
"CE" either; those abbreviations below are this entry's own shorthand, not the book's:
- **General (Preparatory) Exercises ("GPP" — this entry's abbreviation)**: "do not repeat
  the competitive actions as a whole or their separate parts. Other muscle groups take part
  in the work being done. The functional systems of the body are activated but do not
  ensure an increase in results in the competitive exercise." Function: all-round
  development, work capacity, and active rest/restoration. (PDF p. 12, printed p. xi.)
- **Specialized-Preparatory Exercises ("SPE" — this entry's abbreviation; the Glossary's own
  "SPP" label attaches to a related but separately defined "Specialized Exercises" entry,
  see above)**: like general exercises, "do not repeat the competitive actions as a whole
  or in their separate parts. However, they use similar muscle groups in their execution,"
  activating the functions and body systems the main movement depends on, with "identical
  or close to identical regimes of muscle work." (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Specialized-Developmental Exercises ("SDE" — this entry's abbreviation, not the
  Glossary's)**: "repeat the competitive exercise in its separate parts. In executing them,
  one and the same muscle groups participate, together with activation of similar systems
  and organs. They not only repeat the muscle work regime and other systems of the
  body... but also supersede them," and "serve for entry into the state of sports form."
  (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Competitive Exercises ("CE" — this entry's abbreviation, not the Glossary's)**: "the
  acting definition... is 'sport event,' in which the athlete participates in competition,"
  executed either in actual competition or in training as a model/repeat of competitive
  conditions, easier or harder (this definition spans a page break). (PDF pp. 11-12, printed
  pp. x-xi.)
Chapter 2's own intro adds a cross-cutting distinction independent of the four classes: a
**local** exercise (uses separate parts/body links — squat, bench press, standing long
jump, vertical jump) versus a **global** exercise (uses all body links together — the
barbell clean). (PDF p. 75, printed p. 58.)

should differ in transfer value; it only defines them by how much of the competitive
movement each one reproduces. **Inference:** reading the four classes as an ordered
continuum, and connecting that continuum to
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] and the specifist "identical
elements" position in [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]] (more shared
elements with the competitive movement predicting more reliable transfer), is this entry's
own synthesis across sections of the book, not a claim the Glossary or Chapter 2's intro
states in those words. Chapter 2's correlational data (see the claim entries below) can be
read as an empirical test of that inferred prediction, event by event, but the book itself
