=== PDF 024
principle of the “unity of general and specialized preparation”.  If we move away from 
multi-structure, multi-function and multi-system physical exercises, it becomes clear that 
even in the 1960-1970’s, general preparation means were practically not used in the 
training of athletes having different sports qualifications.  
 
In order to not make unsubstantiated statements we will present several examples.  In the 
training of jumpers and throwers, short distance runs were relegated to general 
preparation means.  But this is a specialized-preparatory exercise, in as much as their 
execution develops the speed-strength abilities of the leg flexor and extensor muscles that 
are actively involved in all throws and jumps.  Regardless of this, short distance runs are 
repeated in jumps as they are one of the structural components of the competitive event 
as for example, in the long jump.  Also, in the training of sprinters, jumpers and throwers 
how is it possible to execute a barbell clean or half squat with the barbell as a means of 
general preparation if these muscle groups participate in executing the competitive 
exercise?  The discussion here is related to the flexors and extensors of the legs. 
 
Even more surprising is the classification of middle and long distance running which has 
an aerobic effect, as a means of general preparation.  In execution of the workloads 
coordinated body systems (the nerve-muscle, respiratory, heart-circulatory, and other 
systems) participate even without taking into consideration running technique.   
 
No matter how we “specialize” the means of general preparation, no one and nowhere in 
sports practice is it possible to escape the negative effects when there is development of 
unnecessary muscle groups in one or another sports discipline, especially in speed-
strength events.  Specialists in the sprints, jumps and throws know that extreme 
development of speed-strength abilities of the leg flexor muscles shows up negatively on 
the physical ability of the leg extensors. 
 
This finding is related to the technique of executing the competitive exercise.  Also, 
extreme development of arm strength in the training of a hammer thrower leads to a 
7 
=== PDF 025
decrease in the amplitude of movement of the implement and interferes with the needed 
consecutive inclusion of the basic body links in the work being done. 
 
8 
=== PDF 062
In our study, we did not take exercises from the general developmental group.  Instead 
we took exercises from the specialized-preparatory group or exercises that when 
executed, used similar muscle groups or ensembles of muscles.  Also the training work 
coincided with activation of those same body functions and systems, on which an 
increase in sports results in the competitive exercises depends.  What was the same or 
close to the same was the regimes of muscle work and different functions of other body 
systems.   
 
When it became clear that the means of general preparation do not always create the 
“base”, “foundation”, for growth of sports results in the main event, specialists began to 
carry out tests in specialized-developmental and close to competitive exercises.  These 
exercises appear to be more informative and more “transferable” to the main event.  
Thus, in the track and field throws, with achievement of definite results in throwing 
lighter and heavier implements, it is possible to talk about the possibilities of achieving 
one or another level in throws of the competitive implement (tables 35-40).  Results in 
the 100m run are in conformity with definite test results in the 60 and 150m on one or 
another level.  Other examples can be seen in other track and field disciplines.

Included here are test results in the competitive exercises, executed in lighter and more 
complex conditions.  For example, in the throws, the tests measure results in throws with 
lighter and heavier implements.  In the jumps, the results are recorded in jumps with a 
short approach run.  In cyclical sports, the tests revolve around determining the number 
of segments executed at a given speed and by observing the planned intervals of rest

The reliability of tests that use general preparatory and specialized-preparatory exercises 
still have not been fully confirmed.  This will be tightened up in the near future. 
 
Previous studies in which we tried to determine the exercises that produce a positive 
transfer of training to the competitive exercise are detailed in Chapter 2.  We use those 
that are most frequently used in sports practice.

# Two Test Families: "General" Tests Shared Across Events, "Specialized" Tests Unique to Each

**What it is** — Bondarchuk opens by naming the competitive exercise itself as the
benchmark: determining an exercise's influence on the competitive exercise, "which in all
track and field events, is the most important test" (PDF p. 68, printed p. 51). He then
splits the other tests used to study training transfer into two families (PDF pp. 68-69,
printed pp. 51-52):
- **General tests**: not tests of general-preparatory exercises specifically, but tests
  "used in mixed groups or between groups" — i.e., shared across many events. For
  heart-circulatory/respiratory function, nearly identical tests are used across all of
  track and field (max oxygen uptake on a veloergometer, time-to-exhaustion at max VO2,
  anaerobic threshold). For speed-strength sports, common general tests are the 60m run
  from blocks, barbell snatch, half squat with barbell, standing long jump, vertical jump
  (Abalakov method), triple jump from place, and forward/backward shot throws.
- **Specialized tests**: "In specialized tests for each sport the exercises are very
  similar" and "Each event in this group has its own specific tests" (PDF p. 68, printed
  p. 51) — tests unique to each event's specific demands (lighter/heavier implements in
  throws, shorter approach runs in jumps, varied segment/rest combinations in cyclical
  events).

Of tests generally, he singles out reliability separately from the general/specialized
split: the reliability of tests built from **specialized-developmental exercises** "has
already been shown," while the reliability of tests using general-preparatory and
specialized-preparatory exercises "still have not been fully confirmed. This will be
tightened up in the near future." (PDF pp. 68-69, printed pp. 51-52.)

**Why it works** — The text itself gives no mechanism connecting these two ideas; it simply
asserts that specialized-developmental test reliability "has already been shown" without
citing why. **Inference:** connecting this to
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] — specialized-developmental exercises
sit closest to the competitive event in that transfer chain, so tests built from those same
exercises should track competitive readiness more reliably than tests built
from more general exercises further from the competitive movement.

**When to apply** — When designing or auditing a testing battery, treat the competitive
exercise itself as the single most important test (PDF p. 68, printed p. 51). Below that,
prioritize tests that are themselves specialized-developmental-class movements (the
competitive skill under altered load/distance conditions) over generic strength/power
tests when the goal is tracking competitive readiness specifically; reserve the generic
tests (snatch, squat, vertical jump, etc.) for tracking general physical qualities, which
the author himself says have reliability "not fully confirmed" even though they are
common practice.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is the author's own
methodological framing for the correlational study that follows in Chapter 2, presented
without a formal reliability study of his own two test families in the excerpted pages
(he cites "already been shown" reliability for specialized-developmental tests, but gives
no reference number here). **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and field
athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles
plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not
football, not team sport; the specific listed general tests (barbell snatch, Abalakov
jump, etc.) reflect that era's tools, not necessarily current force-plate/GPS-based
options. **Inference:** applying the general/specialized test distinction to Baylor's own
battery design (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment") is this entry's own
extension in terms of which specific tests to pick, and the claim that the underlying
logic (prefer tests closest to the competitive movement) is "directly portable" is this
entry's judgment, not the author's.

**Example** — **Inference:** for a football wide receiver, a "specialized" test in this
framework would be a competitive-adjacent movement under altered conditions (e.g., a route
run against a lighter or heavier resistance band, or a shortened-approach vertical jump),
while a "general" test would be a standard vertical jump or broad jump shared across every
position group.

**Related** — [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] — the transfer logic
this test-selection framework is built on.
Characteristics of the Tests Used 
 
The study of training transfer mechanisms begins with the fixing of separately taken 
amounts of physical and technical preparation of athletes in the process of using specific 
(or other) exercises and then establishing the inter-relationships between them.  Foremost 
is to determine the influence the exercise has on the competitive exercise, which in all 
track and field events, is the most important test. 
 
As a result of studying multiple literary sources that examined this problem, it was 
concluded that in all speed-strength events and in the endurance group, general and 
specialized tests are used in the training process.  When talk is about general tests, we 
have in mind not those that determine preparation in general preparatory exercises, but of 
similar tests, used in mixed groups or between groups.   
 
For testing the functional state of the heart-circulatory, blood vessel and respiratory 
systems, almost all of the same tests are used in practice in all disciplines of track and 
field.  For example, maximum oxygen uptake is determined on a veloergometer and the 
limits possible while functioning at maximum O2 uptake, anaerobic threshold and others.   
 
In speed-strength sports, they more frequently use tests such as the 60 meter run from a 
low start (blocks), barbell snatch, half squat with the bar on the shoulders, standing long 
jump, vertical jump (according to V.M. Abalakov), triple jump from place, and throwing 
the shot forward, backward.  In specialized tests for each sport the exercises are very 
similar. 
 
In cyclical sports, the most frequently used general tests for endurance are those which 
characterize the level of functioning of the heart-circulatory, blood vessel, and respiratory 
systems (already touched on above).  Each event in this group has its own specific tests. 
 
The reliability of many tests has already been shown.  Foremost in most of these are 
those tests that show the level of preparation in specialized-developmental exercises.  
51

# Three Competing Theories of Training Transfer: Specifist, Generalist, Holistic

**What it is** — Bondarchuk frames the entire theory of training transfer as a debate
between three schools (PDF pp. 20-28, printed pp. 3-11):
- **Specifists** (traced to E.L. Thorndike's "theory of identical elements," cited as
  ref [223]; the source text misgenders Thorndike as "She"): transfer between two
  activities happens only when there is "some kind of concurrence (identicalness) of
  elements" between them. No shared elements, no transfer. (PDF p. 20, printed p. 3.)
  **Inference:** this entry glosses "elements" as muscle groups, coordination structure,
  and biomechanics; the source itself only says "concurrence (identicalness) of elements"
  without spelling those out in this passage.
- **Generalists** (their views "were formed during the years from 1940-1960," per the
  text — not stated to have been dominant): argue for the "unity of general and
  specialized preparation" — build a broad general base first (a multi-year "base stage"
  of 4-6 years), then specialize. Bondarchuk reports this view was later revised once
  research showed general-preparation means only build a base for **low-level** athletes;
  for high-level athletes, transfer to the competitive event comes only through
  specialized-preparation means (citing three refs, [34, 57, 182]). (PDF pp. 22-24, printed
  pp. 5-7.) As that revision took hold, the ratio of training time given to general vs.
  specialized preparation shifted: "If, at the beginning the correlation between the time
  spent on general and specialized preparation was expressed in a 3:1 ratio, it later
  changed in favor of an increased number of specialized preparation means" (PDF p. 23,
  printed p. 6).
- **Holistics**: the body acts as one system, so any exercise affects the whole body's
  systems to some degree (non-specific reactions of the heart-circulatory/respiratory
  systems from any cyclical exercise, e.g. rowing or cycling helping a middle-distance
  runner's aerobic base). Bondarchuk explicitly rejects the holistics' full conclusion
  ("it is not possible to agree with the conclusions of the holistics") but keeps their
  narrower point about non-specific systemic reactions. He also names a deficiency in
  their theory: because holistics indirectly call for training the cardiovascular/
  respiratory systems first to drive neuromuscular adaptation, "the athlete enters the
  highest training state in non-specific exercises at the start and only after this...
  enters a state of sports form in the specific exercises," and "the level of trainedness
  decreases long before entering the state of sports form in the specialized exercises"
  (PDF p. 28, printed p. 11). He notes that jumps, throws, and hurdles coaches agree with
  the holistics on developing physical capacity before technique, formalized as the
  "block" method of separate physical- and technical-preparation blocks (crediting
  Y.V. Verkhoshansky, ref [49]) — but then calls the form/content split underlying it "a
  theoretical and practical error... since they are united in all of their displays" (PDF
  p. 28, printed p. 11); his answer to that error is the principle of conjugated training
  effects (see [[principle--conjugated-training-effects]]). (PDF pp. 26-28, printed pp.
  9-11.)

**Why it works** — The author does not resolve these into a single mechanism in this
section; he uses the three-way split to set up why transfer is contested territory before
he presents his own correlational data in Chapter 2. **Inference:** the specifist view is
the closest ancestor of what this library already holds as
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining, Verkhoshansky/Siff)
and of Verkhoshansky's Principle of Dynamic Correspondence taught in HHPR 5355
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power"); the generalist/holistic debate maps onto
the general-preparation-vs-specialization sequencing question this library already tracks
via Bompa's multilateral development model (vault, not yet cross-checked in this batch).

**When to apply** — Use this three-way split as a diagnostic when reading any other
S&C source's claim about "general" vs "specific" training: ask which of the three
positions it is implicitly taking. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 teaches exercise
selection on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation to
competitive exercises (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`). **Inference:** that is functionally a
generalist-then-specifist sequencing, not a pure specifist position, and this entry gives
Eric's course material a named theoretical lineage (Thorndike/specifist vs. the generalist
sequencing debate) that the transcript itself does not cite.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported, not proven.** This is Bondarchuk's own
literature synthesis of a decades-old Soviet-era academic debate among track and field
scientists, not an independently replicated finding, and the book gives no citation for
exactly how "generalist" views were falsified beyond three bracketed reference numbers
([34, 57, 182]) this ingest did not chase down. **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign
track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four
Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76,
printed p. 59); not football, not team sport. Extending any of the three views to football
programming (e.g., "GPP only helps low-level players") is Inference, not something this
passage states.

**Example** — A coach who says "just build a big general base before specializing" is
taking the classical generalist position Bondarchuk says was revised "with time" once
high-level athlete data showed general work stops producing transfer past a certain
qualification level (PDF p. 23, printed p. 6; the passage does not give a specific decade
for the revision). **Inference:** the Chapter 2 ceiling-effect data in
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] is a plausible empirical echo of this
revision, though the revision text itself cites refs [34, 57, 182], not those tables.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining,
staging) — the specifist position's closest modern-book relative in this library.
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the exercise taxonomy this book actually
uses to operationalize the specifist/generalist tension.

=== PDF 020
The Specifists Viewpoint on the Theory of Training 
Transfer 
 
One of those who established the base for specificity was E. L. Torndyke [223].  She 
called it the theory of identical elements.  In agreement with her, the transfer of training is 
seen when in two types of activities, there is some kind of concurrence (identicalness) of 
elements. Their absence does not make it possible to have transfer.  This appearance is 
completely specific according to its essence. 
 
The transfer of training takes place by using earlier acquired associated ties [284, 287, 
288, 294, 304].  Between them there must be identical elements in a definite order.  The 
theory of identical elements was criticized by many native specialists in the area of 
classical and sports physiology and psychology.  They quoted the learning’s of I. P. 
Pavlov and believed that naturally formed conditioned reflexes lie in the activity of the 
central nervous system.  They do not negate the significance of old associations in the 
systemic activity of the higher segments of the brain.   
 
The influence of the coinciding “working” elements in the process of forming functional 
systems was noted by P.K. Anokhin [7].  According to him, the functional systems are 
only as great as displayed in the existing exercise.  In execution of most exercises, similar 
muscle groups participate.  Besides this, any activity ensures the functioning of one or 
another body system in the process of adaptation that takes place in response to the 
external or internal effect.   
 
Similar muscular groups appear to work in the formation of simple as well as complex, 
physical exercises (according to their coordinational make-up) [25, 26, 79].  This allowed 
several authors to speak of the multi-sided structure of physical exercises [50, 128, 143].  
 
Physical exercises possess multi-functional and multi-system properties.  The multi-
functionality ensures activation of similar organs and body systems [94, 126, 140, 267]. 
3 
=== PDF 022
The Generalists Viewpoint on the Theory of Training 
Transfer 
 
 The viewpoints of the generalists are distinguished from the specifists according to their 
formulation of training transfer.  Generalists recommend several general and specialized 
pedagogical principles which give special attention to harmonious, all-round 
development of the athletes in the process of sports improvement.  The essence of this 
viewpoint is in the principle of unity of general and specialized preparation. Separately, 
each cannot resolve the problems presented before it.  General preparation creates the

The Holistics Viewpoint on the Theory of Training 
Transfer 
 
According to the holistics, the body appears as a single unit and any internal or external 
action affects all of it's systems to a certain degree.  From here it follows that 
development of single abilities cannot take place without the involvement of others.  In 
this, their inter-relationships and consequently their inter-effects always exist.  On the one 
hand, a certain exercise has an influence on the development of another or other physical 
abilities, and on the other hand, ensures the functioning of the entire body as a whole.  
Thus, it is not possible to agree with the conclusions of the holistics.  
 
However, we are interested in significant research on non-specific reactions by the body 
systems with which it is possible to influence the development of specific physical 
abilities of athletes, who specialize in different track and field events or other sports. The 
discussion here is about the multi-functional properties of specific or other exercises 
which bring about similar reactions of the blood vessels, heart-circulatory and respiratory 
systems and allow for an increase in sports results mainly in the cyclic disciplines, 
beginning with the sprints and ending with middle, long, and super-long distances. 
 
Many studies in the theory and methods of physical education substantiate that on the 
higher levels, the above named body systems do not function in the same manner in all 
types of sport.  This is especially true where an increase in achievement depends on a 
definite level of development of speed or specialized endurance.  For example, the 
functional capabilities of the blood vessels, heart-circulatory and respiratory systems can 
be increased equally well, as for example, in training middle distance runners, with the 
use of specialized means or by using exercises from other sports (rowing, cycling, 
swimming, sports games, and so on). 
 
At the present time the positive influence of cyclical sports on increasing the functional 
capabilities of the body systems is generally acknowledged.  However, using other 
9 
=== PDF 027
cyclical sports in cyclical track and field events is limited because of the difficulty of 
transferring them to the main competitive activity.  They also have a negative influence 
on technique of executing the competitive exercise. 
 
For example, in using exercises from cycling or ice skating in the training of sprinters or 
middle distance runners, non-specific muscular groups are developed which can then 
hold back an increase in sports results in the given track and field event.  In this case, we 
come up against both positive and negative transfer of training.   
 
Non-specific reactions of the body systems appear not only in the process of developing 
endurance with the use of different natural but also with non-natural means, in relation to 
the sports event.  However, the single direction of the vegetative functions is fixed in 
developing speed [63, 188].  Similar to this is the display of endurance and when using 
different regimes of muscle work (dynamic and static). 
 
In classic and sports physiology there are many studies that substantiate the fact that in 
the process of developing conditioned reflex reactions, there arises a hotbed of excitation 
in certain nerve centers of the brain that can spread out over “close” and “far” areas [15, 
47, 119, 170]. In the first, “close” instance, nerve impulses appear as some kind of 
separate analyzers as for example, the motor analyzer  [motor movement area] and spread 
out.  In the second, “far” instance, there is inter-analyzational displacement.   
 
It is completely natural that active “close” and “far” areas, which appear as a 
consequence of a generalized distribution or spread of the excitatory-inhibitory impulses, 
appear in a definite form to improve the functional ability of a body system due to non-
specific adaptational changes. 
 
Knowing the regularity of the “breaks” in activeness in the working nerve centers on the 
non-working areas can explain many questions about the transfer of training in the speed-
strength events in track and field and other sports.  Their expression will be accompanied 
10 
=== PDF 028
with great changes in the understanding of the principles not only of training transfer, but 
the very method of training.  All of this is in the future.  
 
Now, we should take note of a major deficiency in the theory of the holistics in that they 
indirectly call for the use of one method of training for increasing the functional 
capabilities of the blood vessels, cardio-vascular and respiratory systems, in order to get 
corresponding adaptational changes in the neuro-muscular system.  This leads to 
disharmony, as the athlete enters the highest training state in non-specific exercises at the 
start and only after this, after several weeks, enters a state of sports form in the specific 
exercises.  It would be possible to ignore this if the functional levels achieved in non-
specific exercises were maintained while the athlete was still achieving corresponding 
increases in his physical preparation in the specific training means.  However, the level of 
trainedness decreases long before entering the state of sports form in the specialized 
exercises. 
 
In the track and field jumps and throws and likewise in the hurdles, there is agreement 
with the holistics that is necessary to first develop the physical capabilities and only after 
this, perfect technical mastery.  Thus the “block” method of constructing cycles of sports 
form development oversees the separate preparatory periods in the blocks of physical and 
technical preparation [49].  Those in agreement with this concept do not believe that 
simultaneously introducing means of technical preparation into the training process 
develops the physical abilities together with improvement of technique. 
 
In these instances, there is a theoretical and practical error working at the base of the 
artificial division of form and content since they are united in all of their displays.  In the 
theory and methods of physical education this unity is expressed in the principle of 
conjugated training effects.  This was proposed in the 1960’s by head coach and scientist 
V.M. Dyachkov [81]. The essence of this method will be looked at further on since it 
provides answers to many questions that require a straight forward understanding of the 
training transfer process. 
 
11

---

# The Principle of Conjugated Training Effects: Physical Preparation and Technique Must Coincide

**What it is** — Physical-ability development and technical-mastery development should
be trained so they "coincide and correspond to the competitive exercise according to
their basic characteristics" rather than as separate tracks. Bondarchuk attributes the
principle to Soviet head coach/scientist V.M. Dyachkov in the 1960s (ref [81]; PDF p. 28,
printed p. 11), and notes it was later "modified by **other specialists** who called it
dynamic correspondence and the principle of resolving motor actions. [157]." The text does
not name who coined the term "dynamic correspondence"; the bracketed ref [157] attaches to
the sentence as a whole, and the very next sentence separately credits U.V. Menkhin [157]
with a specific extension: "the conjugate principle should affect not only the competitive
event, but all the specialized activity as a whole." (PDF p. 29, printed p. 12.) Using gymnastics as
Menkhin's example, the best conjugation requires five things at once: (1) motor qualities
localized to the right muscle groups, (2) motor qualities matching the biodynamic demands
of the skill, (3) transfer into the most common forms of motor activity used for learning
technique, (4) enough work capacity to repeat the skill reliably across a long
competition, and (5) transfer into the competitive combination itself. (PDF p. 29,
printed p. 12.) Bondarchuk says he used this same conjugate principle to build his own
"principle of all-round specialized preparation" (ref [265]): mostly specialized-
preparatory and specialized-developmental exercises, general preparation only for warm-up
and restoration, with each training cycle needing "new" and progressively stronger
special exercises to keep producing adaptation. (PDF p. 30, printed p. 13.)

# Correlation Can Hide a "Tie-In" Exercise That Is Actually Doing the Work

**What it is** — Bondarchuk describes his standard method for the whole book: statistical
analysis (correlation, regression, dispersion, factor analysis, multiple correlation) of
interrelationships between results in different training exercises, using a minimum of
5-6 indices per athlete group because a single pairwise correlation "does not always
reflect the true essence of the interaction." (PDF p. 70, printed p. 53.) He then gives one
illustrative case, which he frames as typical rather than isolated ("we will address only
one of the situations which frequently arise in the process of doing experimental studies
on this problem," PDF pp. 70-71, printed pp. 53-54): a training session using three
exercises, A, B, and C in sequence. After an experiment, results improved in A and C but
not in B. "The coefficient of correlation was sufficiently high between exercises A and B,
which made it possible to think that both exercises had a positive action on one another.
Naturally, the statistical analysis did not bring out the kind of influence exercise B had
on exercise A or C. Based on this, a conclusion was made that exercise B was not
effective." A follow-up experiment dropped B and trained only A and C — and this time
**neither A nor C improved**. Bondarchuk's interpretation: exercise B had a "tie-in
effect," stimulating the positive transfer between A and C even though B itself showed no
measurable within-exercise result. (PDF pp. 70-71, printed pp. 53-54.)

**Why it works** — The author's own explanation for why a single pairwise correlation can
mislead: "the direction and amount of training transfer is dependent first of all on the
integration of activity in the brain, which characterizes the most complex interactions
between the excitatory-inhibitory processes" (PDF p. 70, printed p. 53) — this is also his
stated reason for insisting on a minimum of 5-6 indices per athlete group rather than
single pairwise comparisons. Beyond that stated reason, he defers the tie-in mechanism
itself to "additional studies" that "will resolve this interaction." **Inference:** the
described method (pairwise correlation across a sequence of exercises) is structurally
blind to exactly this kind of three-way interaction, since it only measures direct
pairwise relationships, not an exercise's indirect enabling effect on the relationship
between two *other* exercises — this structural-blindness framing is this entry's own
reading, not the author's stated point.

**When to apply** — Use as a standing caution whenever a program change removes an
exercise because it looks "ineffective" by direct correlation or by the athlete's own
result in that exercise not improving: check whether removing it changes the trajectory
of other exercises in the same session/block before concluding it added nothing.
**Inference:** this is a genuinely underused idea in practical programming, where "cut
what isn't working" is a common simplification heuristic that this example directly
complicates — that practical framing is this entry's own, not the author's.

**Method (applies to every Chapter 2 correlation entry in this book folder):**
questionnaires from native (USSR) and foreign athletes of mixed qualification, carried out
over four Olympic cycles, plus published individual results (PDF pp. 8-9, printed pp.
vii-viii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); "a positive interrelationship between exercises begins
at 0.349" (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59; 0.423 for women's pole vault, PDF p. 111, printed
p. 94); and the data is restricted to training systems **without** steroid use, because
steroid use raises results across all exercises used and not used, masking which exercise
actually drove the transfer (PDF pp. 8-9, printed pp. vii-viii).

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This finding rests on one worked
example, with no stated sample size, no statistical test, and no independent replication
in the excerpted text — it is presented by the author himself as an open question for
future research ("we believe that in the future, additional studies will resolve this
interaction"), not a settled result, even though he frames the underlying situation as one
that "frequently arise[s]." Do not cite this as evidence that any specific exercise
combination has a tie-in effect; treat it only as a methodological caution about what
pairwise correlation studies (including Bondarchuk's own Chapter 2 tables) cannot detect.
Exercises A/B/C are unspecified in the text (not named events or lifts), so there is
nothing concrete to generalize from besides the logical structure of the example and the
Method note above.

**Example** — **Inference:** a strength coach who drops an unweighted plyometric drill
from a sprint-training session because the drill's own jump-height numbers aren't
improving might, per this heuristic, want to check whether removing it also flattens the
sprint-speed gains the program was otherwise seeing — the drill could be a tie-in exercise
even though its own metric looks stagnant.

**Related** — No existing library entry addresses this specific correlation blind spot;
flag for cross-reference if a future ingest (e.g., a sports-statistics or research-methods
source) covers interaction effects or mediation more formally.
=== PDF 008
Correctly understanding the organic inter-relationships between these short and long term 
processes is very important.  Many specialists in the theory and methods of physical 
education have proposed different means of dealing with adaptation which appears as the 
basic survival form of living things.  They give recommendations for the organization of 
the transfer of training without distinguishing the significance of short term and long term 
adaptational restructuring.  But how is it possible to come out against adaptation and 
witness the flow of different levels of adaptational changes? 
  
In sports practice, specialists give outstanding recommendations on the organization of 
the training systems for separate training sessions (means and methods of training, their 
combinations, volume and intensity of training loads and others).  They reveal a decrease 
in effectiveness by changing single complexes of exercises with others in short periods of 
time.  This leads to not finishing single adaptational restructurings in specific body 
systems without which there cannot be any discussion of sports achievement 
improvement.  As a consequence, we  “restructure” other systems that dissect the transfer 
of training.  This switching not only significantly detracts from entering the state of 
sports form, but prevents the transfer of training to take a specific direction, not 
withstanding the creation of unfavorable conditions for the functional systems of the 
body. 
  
In putting together contemporary notions of training transfer, we face significant 
problems.  In the theory and methods of physical education there is little written on this 
topic.  In most cases, they touch on various aspects of training transfer but hardly any of 
the factors that make possible the flow of this process.   Over the last two decades, we 
have systematically collected small increments of experimental material related to the 
positive and negative relationships from the practical exercises used in all the individual 
track and field events.  More than 7,000 athletes having different sports qualifications 
were examined.  Collection of such a large amount of factual material was made possible 
over several decades when the author was with the competitive USSR team.  For 8-10 
months on a daily basis I was with the learning-training groups which included not only 
native, but foreign athletes specializing in different track and field events. 
vii 
=== PDF 009
  
In this book, training transfer is looked at from the point of view of training systems 
without the use of steroids.  When using steroid preparations during the cycles of sports 
form development, at the moment of entering this state, results are increased in all the 
exercises used and in those that were not used in the training. The explanation for this 
regarding the mutual influence of one exercise on other, is practically impossible.  An 
increase in sports results takes place in all used methods of training and with any system 
of training effects.  When training systems without steroids are used, sports results at the 
moment of entering a higher state of sports form do not increase and even decrease.  But 
they always improve with the use of steroids.  The observed increase in sports results is 
always significant. 
  
We didn’t make this finding by chance since the picture of training transfer in the 
exercises when using the two systems mentioned above are distinguishable from each 
other in their roots.  Because of this, before making definite conclusions regarding the 
direction of training transfer, it is necessary to take into consideration only experimental 
material received in the training without the use of steroid preparations.  Only in this case 
can we talk of the true laws of training transfer.   
  
The author sincerely thanks those athletes and coaches who kindly dealt with them in 
their own training but also helped in the collection of experimental material over the 
duration of almost two decades.   
 
 
 
 
 
 
viii 
=== PDF 070
Methods Used to Determine the Effect of Training 
Transfer 
 
As a general rule, all the research touching on the study of training transfer determines 
the amount of interrelationship between separate results of the athletes’ motor activity.  
The number of factors studied depends upon the tests proposed, and the contingent and 
classification of the subjects.  The amount and direction of training transfer are 
determined with the help of statistical analyses.  To do this, correlations, regressions, 
dispersions, factor analyses and multiple correlations are used.  Their effectiveness at this 
time is generally acknowledged and the essence of each is written up in specialized 
papers.   
 
In studying the problems of training transfer, the amount of interrelation between 
achievements in specific training exercises is usually used.  It is usually expressed by the 
coefficient of correlation.   
 
It is absurd to criticize the generally used methods of statistical analysis when some 
researchers have started to use other methods in more recent studies without proposing 
some kind of exchange.  In considering the pertinent facts received in the process of 
experimental studies on the given problem, we will nonetheless take it upon ourselves to 
switch the reader’s attention to the fact that results in speed-strength disciplines, even in 
training elite athletes, do not always reflect the true essence of the interaction between 
different forms of activity and exercises.  This is explained by the fact that the direction 
and amount of training transfer is dependent first of all on the integration of activity in 
the brain, which characterizes the most complex interactions between the excitatory-
inhibitory processes.  Thus, we study the inter-tie-ins with a minimum of 5-6 indices in 
athletes having various sports qualifications. 
 
We will illustrate with one example, which according to our view, reflects the complexity 
of showing the positive inter-tie-ins between exercises.  We will address only one of the 
53 
=== PDF 071
situations which frequently arise in the process of doing experimental studies on this 
problem.  The following schematic of individual training sessions that were characteristic 
of what the athlete used the during the period of developing sports form, consisted of 
three exercises---A, B, and C.  This exercise consecutiveness was used for the duration of 
the entire experiment.  After its conclusion it was shown that sports results increased in 
the first (A) and in the third (C) exercise.  There was no increase in the second (B) 
exercise.   
 
The coefficient of correlation was sufficiently high between exercises A and B, which 
made it possible to think that both exercises had a positive action on one another.  
Naturally, the statistical analysis did not bring out the kind of influence exercise B had on 
exercise A or C.  Based on this, a conclusion was made that exercise B was not effective, 
or did now show a positive influence on exercise A or C.   
 
The aim of the second experiment was to show the correctness of this conclusion.  The 
athletes used only two exercises--A and C for the duration of the study.  After ending the 
experiment it was shown that there was no increase in sports results in these exercises.  
Apparently in the first experiment there was some kind of stimulating action of exercise 
B on exercises A and C.  Thus it is possible to propose a “tie-in” effect of exercise B 
when exercises A and C show positive effects on one another only when together with 
exercise B.  We believe that in the future, additional studies will resolve this interaction 
and propose corresponding methods of analysis.  
 
Additional studies that looked at the problem of training transfer, revolved mainly around 
the problem of finding effective means of training and the interrelationships between 
them [25, 34, 49, 94, 128, 284, 288, 304].  In only some of the papers were the factors 
studied that made this process possible and which ensured it [34, 49, 153, 154].  Studies 
that examined means of training touched on the methodic for developing physical 
abilities (for example, determining the intensity zones, volume of training loads, muscle 
work regimes and others). Also studied was improvement of technique in one or another 
of these aspects (methods, zones of intensity and others).   
54 
=== PDF 076
periods of rest and so on.  Strength, jump, and throw exercises are used sporadically and 
in small amounts, mainly for active rest or for resolving frequent problems that do not 
limit the growth of sports mastery in the competitive event. This conclusion was arrived 
at by specialists through experimental methods. 
 
Positive interrelationships between exercises in each track and field event are determined 
with the use of correlational analyses.  The data used was received mainly through the 
use of questionnaires from native and foreign athletes having different sports 
qualifications.  The questionnaires were carried out over the course of four Olympic 
cycles.  Also analyzed were tests results of individual athletes as recorded in different 
literature sources.  Results of the correlational analyses having a direct relationship to the 
studied factors is presented further on in tables 41-84 and 89-103.  A positive 
interrelationship between exercises begins at 0.349.

---

# A General-Preparation Stage Only "Counts" If It Lasts as Long as the Athlete's Own Sports-Form Cycle

**What it is** — Bondarchuk states that most athletes, after a rest/transition period,
take 2-3 months to enter a state of "sports form" in whatever exercises they are doing,
though some individuals take "4-7 and even 8 months" (PDF p. 39, printed p. 22). A
general-preparation stage/block can only function as a real "base" or "foundation" for the
following specialized stage if it lasts at least as long as that individual's own
sports-form development timeline. He gives his own worked numbers for how this plays out:
in a single-cycle training year, the general-preparation stage runs "on the average, three
months," long enough to let most athletes actually enter sports form in it; in a two-cycle
year, the second general-preparation stage shrinks to "4-6 weeks," and in a three-cycle
year to "2-3 weeks" — both too short for athletes to "have time to enter into full sports
form in the exercises used." (PDF pp. 39-40, printed pp. 22-23.) He gives a
worked counter-example: a sprint/hurdle program with a 10-day general-endurance stage, a
15-day general-strength stage, a 6-8 week speed/speed-endurance stage, and a 2-3 week
entry-into-form stage. Because the first two stages are far shorter than the 2-3+ months
needed to reach sports form, he argues it is "impossible to resolve" real development of
general endurance or general strength in that time — those stages become mere "followers"
(tag-alongs) that prep the body for the next stage, not genuine developmental blocks in
their own right, and sports form only actually begins developing once the speed/speed-
endurance stage starts. (PDF pp. 39-40, printed pp. 22-23.) Only stage, block,
stage-variant, and block-variant methods (which run long enough) can create a real
transferable base; very short 1-3 week rotating stages cannot produce "distant" transfer
of a created base — only "current" transfer is possible under those short-cycle designs
(see [[framework--current-vs-distant-training-transfer]]). (PDF pp. 40-42, printed pp.
23-25.)

**Why it works** — The claim rests on Bondarchuk's premise (stated, not derived here) that
entering "sports form" for a given exercise complex takes a fairly fixed, athlete-specific
duration (2-3 months typical, up to 8 months for some individuals); a stage shorter than
that duration cannot complete the adaptation cycle it is nominally targeting, so whatever
training happens in it is incidental preparation for the next stage rather than a genuine
developmental phase in itself.

**When to apply** — Use as a sanity check on any periodization plan with short (1-3 week)
"phases" labeled by quality (a "strength phase," a "conditioning phase"): ask whether that
phase is actually long enough, for this athlete population, to produce a real adaptation
in that quality, or whether it is functioning only as a short lead-in to the phase after
it. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 teaches training residual effects that set a
retraining cadence — aerobic capacity and max strength need re-exposure roughly every 30
days, speed roughly every 5 days (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27`) — that is a maintenance-cadence claim,
distinct from but complementary to Bondarchuk's claim here about how long an *initial*
developmental stage must run to create a base in the first place.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** The 2-3 month ("4-7 and even 8 month")
sports-form timeline is stated by the author as known "from the literature," without a
specific citation in the excerpted pages. **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track
and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four
Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76,
printed p. 59); not football, not team sport. A college football off-season/summer/fall-camp
calendar is structured very differently (fixed NCAA calendar windows, not free-running
sports-form cycles), so directly importing "your GPP phase must be 2-3 months to count" as
a hard rule for football is Inference — the underlying logic (a phase shorter than the
adaptation timeline for the targeted quality risks being incidental, not developmental)
is more portable than the specific duration numbers.

**Example** — **Inference:** a 2-week "GPP block" before fall camp, by this logic, is very
unlikely to produce genuine general strength or conditioning adaptations in the
Bondarchuk sense; it functions instead as preparation for the next block's actual training
stress, and should be programmed and evaluated as such rather than credited with building
a real strength or conditioning "base."

**Related** — [[framework--current-vs-distant-training-transfer]] — the transfer-timing
model this duration rule directly feeds. [[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]]
(Supertraining, staging) — the general-preparation/work-capacity concept this stage
duration question applies to.
---

# Don't Cut a Strength Exercise Just Because It Stopped Predicting Further Competitive Improvement — Keep It at Lower Volume for Maintenance and Restoration

**What it is** — Having shown across sprints, jumps, and throws that specialized-
preparatory exercises (snatch, clean, squat, bench: see
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] and
[[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]) stop predicting further competitive
improvement past a certain level of mastery, Bondarchuk draws an explicit practical
conclusion rather than leaving it as a pure data finding: "it does not mean that
specialized-preparatory exercises should be excluded from the training. In our view, it is
necessary to use them but to a somewhat lesser volume to maintain the achieved level, as
well as for carrying out restorative measures." He adds two further, separately unhedged
and untested claims (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158): first, that future methods may "widen
the range of transfer with the specialized-preparatory exercises to the competitive and
specialized-developmental exercises"; second, that specialized-preparatory exercises "can
appear as 'stimulational factors' which on the brain level, create conditions for the
transfer to the main movement" even without producing measurable further gains themselves.
Neither claim is tested in the excerpted text.

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given beyond the "stimulational factors... on the brain
level" phrase itself, which the author does not unpack further. This is the author's own
explicit hedge against a naive misreading of his own ceiling-effect data (i.e., "the data
shows no further correlation, therefore cut the exercise" — which he directly warns
against). **Inference:** the "stimulational factor" idea reads as an echo of the "tie-in
effect" from Chapter 1 (see [[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]]),
where an exercise with no measurable direct effect nonetheless enabled other exercises'
gains — but the author does not himself connect these two passages.

**When to apply** — Whenever a program uses Bondarchuk's own ceiling-effect findings (or
any similar correlation-based finding) to justify dropping a strength exercise once an
athlete's numbers plateau relative to competitive results, apply this counter-heuristic:
keep the exercise in the program at reduced volume for maintenance. **Eric's baseline:**
this is consistent with residual strength retention and the roughly-30-day residual
training effect windows this library already tracks (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and
power") and for its restorative/active-recovery role, rather than removing it outright.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is the author's own explicit
practical recommendation, offered as reasoned judgment built on his data rather than as a
separately tested finding in its own right; his two forward-looking claims (widened
transfer range, "stimulational factors") are untested speculation, not data. **Population:**
native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly
from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8,
printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport — the same
population as the ceiling-effect claims this heuristic responds to. Applying "keep it for
maintenance, not for further gains" to
a football strength program's in-season lifting philosophy is Inference, though it is
directly consistent with Baylor's own stated in-season rule of "maintain intensity, reduce
volume" (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`) and its roughly-30-day strength residual
training effect window (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-25`) — two independent sources converging on
the same practical conclusion (reduce, don't eliminate) even though they arrive at it from
different reasoning.

**Example** — **Inference:** a discus thrower whose squat numbers have plateaued relative to further
distance gains should keep squatting at a lower volume/frequency for strength maintenance
and recovery purposes, while shifting the primary developmental emphasis to implement-
weight variation (see [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]), rather
than dropping squats from the program entirely.

**Related** — [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]] and
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] — the data findings this heuristic is
a direct response to. [[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]] —
the Chapter 1 idea (tie-in effect) this heuristic's "stimulational factor" speculation
echoes.

- Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities (e.g., maximal strength work and glycolytic-capacity work) are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block — "you can't ride two horses with one saddle." Compatible qualities are trained together; the rest are trained at a retention dose. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29; week1-lecture.md p.70]
- An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract: lay out the competition calendar, key non-training dates (holidays, exam weeks), and phase-by-phase volume/intensity waves, then adapt the route as circumstances change while still reaching the same destination. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.22-23; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.13-15]
- Training residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue readiness for max-velocity work degrades. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]

# In Endurance Events, Correlation Rises as the Training Distance Nears the Race Distance, and the Transfer Range Shifts Longer as Race Distance Grows

**What it is** — Tables 89-103 (PDF pp. 149-160, printed pp. 132-143) correlate training
segment distances (60m to marathon/50km) against competitive results in the 800m through
marathon and 10/20/50km race walks. Bondarchuk's own summary pattern: "with an increase in
the distance, transfer of physical abilities begins with the longer segments" — 800m and
1500m runners show a cumulative effect starting as short as the 60m segment; men's
steeplechase starts from 600m and women's 3000m from 400m; 5000m runners' range starts
around 600m; marathoners' range starts at 5000m (men) or 3000m (women) — i.e., the
*shortest* segment that still transfers gets longer as the competitive event itself gets
longer (PDF pp. 160-161, printed pp. 143-144). Separately, and stated as a distinct
finding, he adds the book's main correlation-strength regularity for this section: "with a
decrease in the difference between the competitive distances and the test exercises used,
the coefficient of correlation increases" (PDF pp. 160-161, printed pp. 143-144) — the
closer a training segment sits to the race distance, the higher its correlation with the
competitive result tends to run. Elsewhere the same data is described as "with an increase
in the competitive distance, the range of transfer of physical abilities increases" (PDF
p. 145, printed p. 128, discussing 800m vs. 1500m runners) and, in the chapter's own
closing summary, "the range of transfer in the short distances in most endurance events is
significantly wider than in the long distances" (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144) — both
statements are the author's own, given with their own locators; this entry keeps them side
by side rather than picking one.

Representative correlation values: men's 800m showed its strongest correlations with the
400m, 600m, and 1000m segments (0.700-0.912, biggest at 1000m: 0.912, 0.876, 0.905, 0.856;
PDF p. 144, printed p. 127, Table 89), with a sharp drop by the 1500m and further by
3000-5000m; women's 3000m showed positive transfer "on all levels of the segments tested"
except that "transfer to the competitive event from the 100 and 200m runs were
non-existent," strongest with 1000m/1500m/5000m (0.725-0.906, Table 99, PDF p. 146, printed
p. 129). At the ultra-endurance extreme, the pattern breaks: marathoners (and 10km-walk
women / 50km-walk men) show **no** cumulative effect from segments *longer* than the
competitive distance. The author gives this as two separate sentences, not one
"because"-clause: "In these cases, it is not possible to observe the presence of the
cumulative effect with distances that are longer than the competitive event. In sports
practice similar tests do not exist." (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144.) Race-walkers'
running-distance correlations (5000m/10000m run vs. walk results) were uniformly weak
(0.354-0.400), far below their same-discipline walk-distance correlations (up to 0.800+).
(PDF pp. 148-149, printed pp. 131-132.)

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk attributes the general pattern to "the specifics of the
interaction of systems involved in the training effect" — different aerobic/anaerobic-
alactate/anaerobic-lactate energy-system demands at different distances (general systemic
reactions) plus the individual athlete's short- and long-term adaptational responses
(specific reactions). (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144.) He does not fully resolve *why* the
transfer range widens with distance beyond this general systems-interaction language.
**Inference:** one possible reading is that longer events draw on a broader mix of energy
systems and pacing demands, so a wider band of training distances can stress a
physiologically relevant system for that event; this interpretation is this entry's own
reading, not stated by the author, and no outside exercise-physiology source was checked
in this ingest to confirm it.

**When to apply** — Use as historical support for distance-specific training range
selection: shorter competitive events (800m-1500m) can be trained effectively with a
narrower, shorter set of segment distances; longer events (5000m-marathon) benefit from
(and require) a wider spread of training distances, from well below race distance up to
race distance itself, to cover the full transfer range this data shows. **Eric's
baseline:** HHPR 5355 already treats aerobic-system training for speed-power athletes as
mainly serving inter-effort recovery rather than distance capacity, kept below anaerobic
threshold at roughly a 1:1-1:2 work:rest ratio (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and
energy systems," citing `week3-lecture.md p.51`) — this book's population is exclusively
dedicated distance-event specialists, a very different training context from a
speed-power athlete's incidental aerobic work, so this entry's distance-range findings
should not be imported into football conditioning design without that distinction in mind.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** **Population:** native (USSR) and
foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires
over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF
p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport; the specific segment distances and
correlation values are dataset-specific. This entry covers **running/walking segment
distances only** — it says nothing about strength, jump, or throw-exercise transfer to
endurance events (not tested in this chapter). Applying "wider transfer range for longer
events" to a team-sport repeated-sprint or intermittent-endurance context (football's
actual endurance demand, per `method-baseline.md`'s energy-systems framing) is Inference:
football conditioning is not a single continuous-distance competitive event in the way
every sport in this dataset is.

**Example** — **Inference:** a 10,000m runner's program using training distances from
600m intervals up to marathon-length long runs is well-supported by this data's
transfer-range findings; a marathoner's program should not expect any additional transfer
benefit from segments longer than the marathon itself, since no such segment exists to
test or train.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — general classification
these segment distances fall under (specialized-developmental to competitive, depending on
how close the segment is to full race distance).

=== PDF 144
 
We will begin with middle distance runners.  They use segments anywhere from 60-
100m up to 10-15km in length.  Runners specializing in the steeplechase (3,000m with 
hurdles) 5,000m and 10,000m (both men and women) as well as women specializing in 
the 3,000m run, use distances from 100m to 20-30km.  Marathoners use distances from 
400m – to several 10s of kilometers.  Also used are training loads lasting more than 2hrs.   
 
In sports walking, running as well as walking are used for short and long distances.  For 
women specializing in the 10km walk, the distances vary from 1-20km, and for 20 and 
50km men walkers—from 1-30km.  The latter as well as marathoners, do training work 
lasting more than 2hrs.   
 
After competition a general picture of the means and methods of developing anaerobic 
and aerobic abilities used in cyclical sports that require endurance is revealed.  In general 
terms, we will present experimental material which shows the range of transfer of the 
physical abilities in the middle, long and super long running distances as well as in sports 
walking for the 10 (women), and 20 and 50km (men) events. 
 
In the men’s and women’s 800m run, there is a range of transfer of physical abilities 
beginning with the 60m run from a low start and ending with the 5000m run (tables 89, 
97).  The latter distances with the men, had a place on two levels of sports mastery 
(1:56:00-2:00:00 and 1:52:00 1:56:00) and with the women, on one level (2:15:00-
2:20:00).  The greatest amounts of correlational interrelationship were fixed in the 400, 
600, and 1000m runs.  In performers of both sexes, the correlation varied from 0.700-
0.900.  In men, the biggest transfer was with the 1000m run (0.912, 0.876, 0.905, 0.856).  
A sharp decrease in the amount of correlational interrelationship was observed in the 
1500m run in men and women.  A weak interrelationship was seen with the 3000 and 
500m runs. 
 
The range of transfer of physical abilities in the men’s 1500m run begins with the 60m 
segment and ends with the 5000m distance.  The cumulative effect has a place on all 
127 
=== PDF 145
levels of sports mastery.  In women, as in the men, the range of transfer begins with the 
60m but ends on the 10,000m distance.  In the latter case it appears on three of the five 
levels of sports mastery.  The greatest amount of correlational interrelationship is 
observed in participants of both sexes in the 800, 1000 and 3000m runs (table 90, 98).   
 
Results of the correlational analysis of 800 and 1500m runners shows that with an 
increase in the competitive distance, the range of transfer of physical abilities increases.  
Thus, for men participants in the “long sprint” (800m) transfer is seen with the 5000m 
distance, and in the women specializing in the 1500m run, transfer has a place in the 
10,000m distance.  In the 800m runners greatest transfer was seen with the 600 and 
1000m and with the 1500m runners, in the 800, 1000, and 3000m runs. 
 
In comparing the amounts of interrelationship between results in the competitive running 
distance with women specializing in the 800 and 1500m, we came to the conclusion that 
in the 800m runners, results in the 1500m run were more transferable to the competitive 
event (coefficient of correlation varied from 0.657-0.788), than in the 1500m runners 
(from 0.380-0.652).   
 
Analysis of the results of the ten strongest 800 and 1500m runners in the world 
throughout the history of track and field, shows that the world record holders in the 
1500m run frequently demonstrate a higher level of achievement in the 800m run than 
world record holders in the 800m run in the 1500m distance.  Only one athlete, S. Coe 
was able to have a world record in both distances. 
 
The range of transfer of physical abilities in steeplechase runners begins with the 600m 
run (three levels of sports mastery) and ends with the 10,000m run.  A positive transfer is 
not observed with results in the 100 and 400m runs.  The most transferable were the 
3,000 and 5,000m runs.  Here the coefficient of correlation in four instances was greater 
than 0.700 and in one---0.800 (table 91).  In the 600, 800, 1,000, 1,500 and 10,000m runs, 
the coefficient was very low (from 0.356-0.497), which signifies the weak 
interrelationship between the studied indices.  However, some of the strongest athletes 
128 
=== PDF 146
show high sports results not only in the 5,000m distance but in the 1,500, 3,000, and 
10,000m.   Note that the leading runner, H. Rono, set the world record in the 5,000, 
10,000m and steeplechase in his time. 
 
In the women’s 3,000m the range of transfer of physical abilities is somewhat greater 
(table 99), than with the steeplechase runners.  Here it begins with the 400m run and ends 
with the 10,000m run.  The positive interrelationship had a place on all levels of the 
segments tested.  Most transfer was in the 1,000, 1,500, and 5,000m runs.  The 
coefficients of correlation varied from 0.725-0.906.  Transfer to the competitive event 
from the 100 and 200m runs were non-existent.  Practice substantiates that many of the 
strongest 3,000m women runners in the world (Olympic and world champions and record 
holders) showed the greatest results in the mixed distances.  Thus, the former world 
record holder in this distance, T. Kazankina, two time Olympic champion in the 1500m 
and one time winner in the 800m and American M. Decker who was world champion in 
the 1500 and 3000m runs.   
 
The range of transfer of physical abilities in the 5000m run, both in the men as in the 
women, begins with the 600m run (table 92, 100).  In men, transfer appears on all levels 
of sports mastery and in women, only on two (16.00-16.30 and 16.30-17.00min).  The 
cumulative effect is also seen in the marathon results. Here it is observed both in the men 
as in the women only on two levels of sports mastery.  The 800, 1000, 1500, 3000 
10,000m and half marathon, show a positive transfer taking place on all levels of sports 
mastery. The greatest transfer appears in the 3,000 and 10,000m run.  In men, the 
coefficient of correlation in these distances was somewhat higher than in the women.  
 
Results of the correlational analysis substantiates that the range of transfer of physical 
abilities in athletes specializing in the 10,000m run begins with results in the 600m run 
and ends with results in the marathon (table 93, 101).  The first distance has a place on 
two consecutive levels (28.00-28.30 and 28.30-29.00min), and the second, on all levels 
from 28.00-34.00min.  In the women, the range of transfer is somewhat less than in the 
men.  It begins with results in the 1,500m run.  However, runners of both sexes show that 
129 
=== PDF 148
woman, I. Christianson was world record holder in the marathon and also in the 5,000 
and 10,000m.  
 
As a rule, most of the strongest world marathon runners show high results in the 10,000m 
run.  This is explained first of all by the fact that almost all of them began by specializing 
in long distance running and only later, after the passage of time, went over to the 
marathon.  In bettering their sports results in the marathon they also improved their 
results in the 10,000m run.  But none of them set a record at this distance during this 
time.  Besides this, in most cases the time (year) of setting personal bests in both 
distances did not coincide. 
 
In athletes specializing in the 10km walk, the cumulative effect was fixed at two running 
distances (5,000 and 10,000m) and in the 1 and 5km walks (table 103).  The cumulative 
effect was absent only on one level of sports results (the 5,000m run).  In the running 
exercises the coefficient of correlation in all cases was very low---from 0.354 up to 0.387 
which shows the weak interrelationship between indices in the 5,000 and 10,000m run 
with the competitive event.  In the 1km walk, it varied on the level of 0.700-0.800.  In the 
5km walk, the coefficient of correlation in three cases exceeded 0.800 and in one, 0.700.   
 
The range of transfer of physical abilities in athletes specializing in the 20km walk begins 
with special developmental exercises and results in the 1km walk and ends with results in 
the 50km walk (table 95).  The cumulative effect also has a place in the 10,000m run.  
The biggest coefficients of correlation were fixed in the 10km walk and the smallest in 
the run at this distance—from 0.354-0.387.  In the 50km walkers, the transfer of physical 
abilities to the 1km walk is observed on two levels of sports mastery and in the 5, 10, and 
20km walks on all levels (table 96).  Most transfer was with the results in the 10 and 
20km walks.  A weak correlation of the interrelationship was observed with indices in the 
10,000m run. 
 
Results of the correlational analysis of athletes specializing in the 20 and 50km walks 
show that in the first group, results in the 10 and 50km have the greatest transfer while 
131 
=== PDF 149
for the second group (50km) results in the 10 and 20km walks.  Almost the same was the 
cumulative effect with achievements in the 10,000m run and 1km walk.  Here, the 
coefficient of correlation in all instances did not go above 0.400, which indicates the 
weak interrelationship between them.

In this section of experimental material related to the study of runners specializing in 
middle, long and ultra long distances, the correlational interrelationships between results 
in the specialized-developmental and competitive events, show that with an increase in 
the distance, transfer of physical abilities begins with the longer segments.  Thus, in the 
800 and 1500m runs, the cumulative effect is already seen with indices in the 60m run.  
In the men’s steeplechase it appears with results in the 600m run and in the women’s 
3000m run with indices in the 400m run.   
 
A positive transfer of physical abilities with 5000m runners was fixed with results in the 
600m run.  In the longer distances, in the men, the cumulative effect was seen in the 
600m run and with the women, with results in the 1000m run.  In men marathoners the

3000m. 
 
In middle distance runners, the ranger of transfer of physical abilities ends at the 5,000m 
distance and in the 3,000m run with women and steeplechase for men, at 10,000m.  With 
long distance runners the cumulative effect was seen with indices in the marathon run.  
With athletes specializing in the 10 (women) 20 and 50km (men) walk, the transfer of 
physical abilities begins with indices in the 1km walk.   
 
Results of the correlational analysis also substantiate that in most events requiring the 
display of endurance, with a decrease in the difference between the competitive distances 
143 
=== PDF 161
and the test exercises used, the coefficient of correlation increases.  This is related to both 
the short and long segments in relation to the competitive event.  The difference is that 
the range of transfer in the short distances in most endurance events is significantly wider 
than in the long distances.  The exceptions here appear to be athletes specializing in the 
marathon, women in the10km walk and men in the 50km walk.  In these cases, it is not 
possible to observe the presence of the cumulative effect with distances that are longer 
than the competitive event.  In sports practice similar tests do not exist.   
 
The greatest range of transfer of physical abilities in all events requiring endurance, is 
explained by the specifics of the interaction of systems involved in the training effect and
