# Jump-from-a-Short-Run-Up Is the Single Most Transferable Assistance Exercise for Every Jump Event; High Jump Is the Outlier

**What it is** — Tables 61-68 (PDF pp. 104-112, printed pp. 87-95) correlate running,
jumping, and strength/throw exercises against long jump, high jump, triple jump, and pole
vault results, men and women. Across long jump, triple jump, and pole vault, **all**
running and jumping exercises showed a cumulative positive effect; the two throwing
exercises (shot forward/backward) showed essentially none. The single strongest, most
consistent exercise across event types was the **jump/vault with a short run-up**: long
jumpers' correlation to a short-approach jump ran 0.721-0.890 for men, 0.830-0.967 for
women (Tables 61-62); triple jumpers' short-run-up triple jump ran 0.890-0.954 for men,
0.700-0.906 for women (Tables 65-66); pole vaulters' short-run-up vault ran 0.706-0.845
for men, 0.788-0.865 for women (Tables 67-68). Women's 10-fold-jump-from-place row in Table 64 is 0.886, 0.965,
0.905, 0.890, 0.865 across the five qualification bands — a range of **0.865-0.965**, not
0.886-0.965 as an earlier draft of this entry stated (taking only the first two values'
span instead of the row's true min/max). The men's 10-fold row (Table 63) is 0.876-0.945.
**A positive interrelationship begins at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59) throughout this
book; all values cited here clear that threshold.

**High jump and the source's own internal contradiction — kept visible, not resolved.**
Two passages describe high jump's correlations differently, and this entry records both
rather than picking one: PDF p. 112 (printed p. 95) says "in all cases, a weak
interrelationship between the test results was observed on the 0.400 level" for men's and
women's high jump generally. But PDF p. 105 (printed p. 88), describing the same Tables
63-64, says "a correlational interrelationship was observed in all running and jumping
exercises," with jump exercises running much stronger than the running exercises: the
prose there gives the vertical jump with a short run-up (matching the 10-fold-jump row's
values, see the exact-match note below) at 0.876-0.945 (men) / 0.865-0.965 (women), and
Tables 63-64's 100m-from-blocks row runs roughly 0.60-0.71 across both sexes — not a
uniform 0.400-level weak relationship. The source contradicts itself on how weak high
jump's correlations actually are; do not resolve it in a future entry without checking
the original Russian or a second translation.

**Note on the 0.876-0.945/0.865-0.965 figures above:** the prose at PDF p. 105 (printed
p. 88) names them "the vertical jump with a short run-up," but those exact figures match
the "10-fold jump from place" row in Tables 63-64 (men 0.876-0.945, women 0.886-0.965; the
women's true range per the row's five values is 0.865-0.965, see above), not the row
literally labeled "Jump from a short run-up" in the same tables (men 0.706-0.805, women
0.680-0.808, which the prose separately describes as merely "sufficiently high"). This may
be a translation/editing inconsistency between the prose's exercise name and the table's
row label; do not assume which one is authoritative without checking the original Russian
or a second translation.

**Snatch, corrected.** The prior version of this entry said the barbell snatch "showed
almost no transfer anywhere in this section except isolated single-level effects." The
source states more transfer than that: for men's pole vault, "a positive transfer was
observed on all levels of sports results in the barbell snatch and in the half squat with
the barbell on the shoulders" (PDF p. 111, printed p. 94); more broadly, "in the second
strength exercise (barbell snatch) the cumulative training effect had a place on several
levels of sports mastery in most events except for the women's high jump and men's triple
jump" (PDF p. 112, printed p. 95). Men's long jump snatch correlations ran 6.5-7.3m level
(PDF p. 103, printed p. 86). The half squat with barbell transferred even more
consistently — all levels, both sexes, in high jump and pole vault (PDF p. 112, printed
p. 95).

**Women's pole vault exception.** The single strongest correlation for women pole vaulters
was not the short-run-up vault: it was the 60m run from blocks (0.856, 0.886), above the
short-run-up vault itself (0.788, 0.865) (PDF p. 111, printed p. 94) — an exception to
"short-run-up is the single strongest exercise across event types" worth carrying alongside
that generalization. (PDF pp. 104-113, printed pp. 87-96.)

**Why it works** — The tables report these correlations without explaining them.
**Inference:** reading this through [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] and
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]], the short-run-up version of each
event's own competitive movement is itself a specialized-developmental exercise (repeats
the competitive action's parts under an altered, easier condition), which would place it
closer to the competitive event than general-preparatory sprint and strength exercises —
but this connection is this entry's own reading, not the author's stated explanation, and
the internal high-jump contradiction above shows the pattern is not clean even on the
author's own numbers. **Inference:** the high jump's approach and takeoff (curved run,
back-to-the-bar rotation) differs enough biomechanically from a straight-line sprint that
raw straight-ahead sprint speed may simply share fewer "identical elements" with it than
with long jump, triple jump, or pole vault approaches — this technique speculation is this
entry's own; the author does not state which high-jump technique his athletes used.

**When to apply** — When selecting assistance work for a jump-event athlete, this data
supports prioritizing a short-approach version of the competitive jump itself as the
highest-value transfer exercise, over generic sprint times or barbell strength numbers,
with the explicit exception of high jump, where multi-jump (10-fold) and short-approach
vertical jump work outperformed straight sprint speed as a predictor.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** **Population:** native (USSR) and
foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires
over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF
p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport. **Inference:** the "high jump breaks
the pattern" finding may be specific to whichever high-jump technique (Fosbury flop,
straddle, or other) Bondarchuk's athletes used; the text does not state which technique,
so this is speculation, not a stated limitation. Applying any of these specific exercise
priorities to a football skill (e.g., a receiver's high-point jump) is Inference — no
football population data exists in this source.

**Example** — **Inference:** a long jump program prioritizing short-approach full-technique
jumps (at reduced run-up length) as the top assistance tool, alongside sprint work, is
well-supported by this data; the same prioritization for a high jumper should shift toward
short-approach vertical/10-fold jump work rather than assuming sprint speed transfers the
same way, though the source's own internal contradiction on high jump above means this
recommendation is less clean than it looks.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification
explaining why the short-run-up version outperforms more general exercises.
[[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]] — the parallel finding for
sprinters using jump exercises as assistance work (the reverse direction of transfer).

**Why it works** — The tables report these correlations without explaining them.
**Inference:** reading this through [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] and
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]], the short-run-up version of each
event's own competitive movement is itself a specialized-developmental exercise (repeats
the competitive action's parts under an altered, easier condition), which would place it
closer to the competitive event than general-preparatory sprint and strength exercises —
but this connection is this entry's own reading, not the author's stated explanation, and
the internal high-jump contradiction above shows the pattern is not clean even on the
author's own numbers. **Inference:** the high jump's approach and takeoff (curved run,
back-to-the-bar rotation) differs enough biomechanically from a straight-line sprint that
raw straight-ahead sprint speed may simply share fewer "identical elements" with it than
with long jump, triple jump, or pole vault approaches — this technique speculation is this
entry's own; the author does not state which high-jump technique his athletes used.

**When to apply** — When selecting assistance work for a jump-event athlete, this data
supports prioritizing a short-approach version of the competitive jump itself as the
highest-value transfer exercise, over generic sprint times or barbell strength numbers,
with the explicit exception of high jump, where multi-jump (10-fold) and short-approach
vertical jump work outperformed straight sprint speed as a predictor.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** **Population:** native (USSR) and
foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires
over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF
p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport. **Inference:** the "high jump breaks
the pattern" finding may be specific to whichever high-jump technique (Fosbury flop,
straddle, or other) Bondarchuk's athletes used; the text does not state which technique,
so this is speculation, not a stated limitation. Applying any of these specific exercise
priorities to a football skill (e.g., a receiver's high-point jump) is Inference — no
football population data exists in this source.

**Example** — **Inference:** a long jump program prioritizing short-approach full-technique
jumps (at reduced run-up length) as the top assistance tool, alongside sprint work, is
well-supported by this data; the same prioritization for a high jumper should shift toward
short-approach vertical/10-fold jump work rather than assuming sprint speed transfers the
same way, though the source's own internal contradiction on high jump above means this
recommendation is less clean than it looks.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification
explaining why the short-run-up version outperforms more general exercises.
[[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]] — the parallel finding for
sprinters using jump exercises as assistance work (the reverse direction of transfer).

=== PDF 103
Transfer of Physical Abilities in the Jumps When Using 
Different Exercises 
 
Considering the specifics of training in the track and field jumps, we studied the 
influence of different runs (sprints), jumps, throws and strength exercises that are most 
frequently used in sport practice and their relationship to the main movement (event). 
 
The system of training jumpers has been made more complex in the last 10 years 
considering the duration of the cycles of developing sports form during which a large 
number of specialized exercises are used together with repetition of the competitive event 
and its’ separate segments [42, 81,212].  The percentage of special exercises, in 
comparison to the total volume of training time, was 50-60%.  Improving the competitive 
event by repeating the entire movement comprised 20-30% of the total time.  A frequent 
exception to this were high jumpers whose total training loads in the competitive event 
training were 10-20% greater than athletes specializing in other jump events.  The percent 
of strength and throwing exercises varied between 15-25%. 
 
Now we will analyze the factual material touching on the problem of training transfer of 
different exercises to the competitive exercise.  We will begin with the men’s and 
women’s long jump.  The correlational analyses (tables 61,62) substantiate that the 
positive cumulative effect is observed when all types of run and jump exercises are used 
and the two throwing exercises—throwing the shot forward and backward are absent.  
The greatest interrelationships were seen in the jumps with a short approach run, in the 
30m run with a flying start and in the ten-fold jump from place.  In the barbell snatch 
with men, a positive training transfer was observed when the sports results were from 
6.5-7.3m and in women from 5.0-6.1m.  Several others were seen in the half squat with 
the barbell on the shoulder.  In the women, the cumulative effect appeared on all levels of 
sports results and in the men only on three, from 6.5-7.6m.

Correlational analyses in the specialized-preparatory, specialized-developmental and 
competitive exercises allowed us to show a general picture of transfer of physical abilities 
from one means of training to another.  It was seen that in all the jumpers, the greatest 
amount of interrelationship was observed between results in the jumps using a short and 
full (competitive) approach run.  The coefficient of correlation varied most frequently 
between 0.750-0.900.   
 
High amounts of transfer of the cumulative effect was seen in all the jump exercises in 
the long jumpers, triple jumpers, and pole-vaulters.  What is pertinent to the men and 
women athletes specializing in the high jump, is that in all cases, a weak interrelationship 
between the test results was observed on the 0.400 level.  
 
In we compare the amounts of correlational interrelationship between single and triple 
jumps (vertical jump, long jump, and triple jump from place) and multiple jumps (five-
and ten-fold) then it can be seen that the second form of exercises (multiple jumps) have 
a greater number of cases in which the correlation is higher than with the first exercises. 
 
The most transferable strength exercise is the half squat with the barbell on the shoulders.  
Here, both with the men and women, in the high jump and in the pole vault as well as 
with the women in the long jump and triple jump, the transfer of physical abilities is 
observed on all levels of sports mastery.  In the men’s long jump it appears on three 
levels and in the triple jump,--- on four.  In the second strength exercise (barbell snatch) 
the cumulative training effect had a place on several levels of sports mastery in most 
events except for the women’s high jump and men’s triple jump.

# Bondarchuk Publishes 40 Normative Tables Linking Assistance-Exercise Results to Competitive-Result Bands, by Age and Qualification

**What it is** — Tables 1-34 run PDF pp. 44-60, printed pp. 27-43 (this ingest sampled
representative tables rather than transcribing all 34); Tables 35-40 plus surrounding
prose run PDF pp. 61-64, printed pp. 44-47 — the section is 40 tables, not 34, and the
last six were not covered by an earlier draft of this entry. Tables 1-34 give normative
"model characteristics": for a given competitive-result band (e.g., 100m in 10.00-10.20s
vs. 10.80-11.00s), a matching range of expected results in assistance exercises. Examples
pulled directly: **Table 1** ties 100m sprint splits (10m through 100m segments) to
five 100m-time bands. **Table 2** ties speed-strength markers (standing long jump,
triple/5-fold/10-fold jump from place, single-leg and alternate-leg jumps for time) to
those same five 100m bands — e.g., a 10.00-10.20s sprinter should stand-long-jump
3.10-3.30m, a 10.80-11.00s sprinter 2.70-2.90m. Similar tables exist for 200m, 400m,
women's 100m hurdles, and age-banded (15-16 / 17-18 / 19+) versions for 400m men and
women across successive preparatory/competitive periods (Tables 10-14). Table 8 also
gives named-athlete individual data (L. Evans, T. Smith, V. Markin, and others) with
columns for 100m result, 200m result, a "repeated results in the 200m" value, the 400m
result, the difference between the repeated-200m value and the 400m result, and a "Speed
Reserve" column (e.g. L. Evans: 100m 10.2s, 200m 20.3s, repeated-200m 40.6s, 400m 43.86s,
difference 3.26s, Speed Reserve 0.765). The table does not state how "Speed Reserve" is
calculated. **Inference:** it reproduces cleanly as (400m time / 4) minus 100m time —
L. Evans: 43.86/4 - 10.2 = 0.765; T. Smith: 44.1/4 - 10.2 = 0.825; D. Carr: 46.2/4 - 10.4 =
1.150 — every row this ingest checked against that formula matched Table 8's printed
value. The book itself does not give this derivation. (PDF pp. 44-49, printed pp. 27-32.)

**Tables 35-40** give expected distance differences between the competitive implement and
lighter/heavier implements in the throws, by sex — e.g. men's hammer, 7.260kg vs. 5kg:
+13m (±3.4); 7.260kg vs. 10kg: -16m (±1.3) (Table 35, PDF p. 62, printed p. 45); similar
tables exist for shot, discus, and javelin (men and women). (PDF pp. 62-64, printed
pp. 45-47.)

**Norms were built two ways.** "Individually-selected": each exercise's best mark is drawn
from whichever of the ten strongest athletes in the world/country produced it (so
different exercises in the same row can come from different athletes). "Collective-
average": the ten best athletes' marks in each exercise are summed and averaged, and that
average serves as the target; this is the method "used most frequently." (PDF p. 61,
printed p. 44.)

**The author's own not-causal caveat.** Bondarchuk states this limitation himself, not
only as this entry's inference: test levels in these exercises let a coach "judge the
speed-strength abilities of each individual separately. However, this does not to any
degree determine the amount of increase in the competitive exercises (events)" (PDF p. 61,
printed p. 44). Later in the chapter he restates it for the specialized-developmental
exercises specifically: "achieving a definite level of test results, even in the
specialized-developmental exercises, does not guarantee an increase in sports achievement
in the main event" (PDF p. 65, printed p. 48).

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given; these are purely descriptive normative
benchmarks compiled from the author's dataset, presented as targets an athlete "should"
hit at a given competitive level, not as evidence of a causal relationship (the author's
own caveat above makes this explicit, not just an inference). **Inference:** this
functions the same way modern S&C "standards tables" (e.g., a vertical-jump-by-40-
time chart) function — useful as a rough talent-identification or gap-analysis tool, not
as proof that improving the assistance-exercise number will improve the competitive time.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** `method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment"
(citing `performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2`) names a live gap in
Baylor's own testing program: a vendor-organized data dictionary that lacks per-sport
GPS/load thresholds, not normative test tables specifically. **Inference:** Bondarchuk's
banded, qualification-linked table format (multiple assistance exercises per
competitive-result band, banded by age where relevant) is one possible model for building
that kind of sport-specific normative reference, even though the specific numbers here are
1970s-80s Soviet track and field data and not directly usable for a 2026 football roster.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported**, and only as a description that these
tables exist and roughly what they show — this entry does not treat any individual number
as validated for use as a current standard. **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track
and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four
Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76,
printed p. 59; refs [52], [74], [75] specifically for these tables); not football, not team
sport; the specific split times, jump distances, and the Table 8 "speed reserve" formula
are Inference if applied to any other sport or era without re-derivation. This ingest did
not transcribe all 40 tables (only Tables 1-14 and 35-40 were pulled in full); a future
batch revisiting this chapter should note that gap before citing a
table number 15-34 that was not directly checked here.

**Example** — A recruiting or testing-standards project comparing "where does our sprinter
sit" could borrow the *format* (competitive-result band -> matching assistance-exercise
range, split by age where useful) from Table 2/10-14 without adopting the actual Soviet-
era numbers.

**Related** — No existing library entry covers normative benchmark tables directly; see
Eric's own gap analysis in `method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," for the live
Baylor need this table format could inform.

In working out model characteristics in all groups in the track and field disciplines, 
specialists used individually-selected and collective-average methods.  The first of them 
oversees selection of the individuals best test scores and the level achieved by one of the 
ten strongest athletes in the country or world in this or another track and field discipline.  
For example, one athlete shows the best result in the snatch and another in the standing 
long jump and a third in the squat with the barbell on the shoulders and so on.   
 
In using the second method, the test scores for each of the exercises are added up, as for 
example, the results of the ten best athletes in the world are summed up and then 
averaged.  The average result then serves as a base score for the athletes who want to 
achieve this sports result in the competitive exercise on the world standard level. 
 
The collective-average method is used most frequently in determining the test scores of 
athletes having different sports qualifications.  In the beginning, test scores are 
established for the means of general preparation, as this encompasses the stage method of 
constructing cycles of sports form development.

# Specialized-Developmental Runs (Flying 30m, Blocks 30-200m) Correlate Strongly with Sprint/Hurdle Competitive Results

**What it is** — Tables 41-50 (PDF pp. 78-87, printed pp. 61-70) report correlation
coefficients between competitive results and other specialized-developmental/competitive
run distances, for men's and women's 100m, 200m, 400m, 110m/400m hurdles (men) and
100m/400m hurdles (women), each split by "high level" vs. "low level" athlete
qualification (the table note: high-level in the numerator, low-level in the denominator
for these specific tables — Tables 41-50 only; see the reversed convention noted in
`_book.md` for the throws tables). Bondarchuk's own summary: "the coefficients of
correlation in most cases are in the range of 0.700-0.800" (PDF p. 87, printed p. 70).
Representative individual values pulled directly (high-qualification/low-qualification):
100m runners' 30m-flying-start correlated 0.678/0.778 with the 30m-from-blocks segment and
0.756/0.876 with the 100m-from-blocks segment (Table 41); 110m hurdlers' 110m-hurdles
result correlated only 0.562/0.420 with the 200m-from-blocks segment, the weakest pairing
involving the competitive 110m hurdles result (Table 44 has still-lower pairings among its
other rows, e.g. 30m-from-blocks vs. 150m at 0.390/0.426 and vs. 200m at 0.414/0.361, PDF
p. 81, printed p. 64); 400m hurdlers' 400m-hurdles result correlated as high as
0.890/0.806 with the 600m-from-a-high-start segment (Table 45). **A positive
interrelationship between exercises begins at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59).

**Why it works** — The tables report the correlations without explaining them. **Inference:**
reading this through
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] and
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — these are all specialized-developmental
or competitive-class exercises (shorter/longer runs at or near race intensity), sharing
most of the sprint or hurdle event's biomechanics and energy-system demands, which would
predict the high correlation observed — but this connection is this entry's own reading,
not a claim the author makes for this specific table set.

**When to apply** — Use as historical evidence that assistance runs at varied distances
(flying starts, sub-maximal and supra-maximal segment lengths) are a reliably transferable
training tool for sprint/hurdle athletes, supporting programs that use varied-distance
sprint work rather than only full-distance reps. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355's
linear-sprint testing already uses split-time interpretation by physical quality (0-10m
acceleration, 30-40m speed) rather than total time alone (`method-baseline.md`, "Speed
and sprint," citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`). **Inference:** this book's high
segment-to-total correlations support treating those splits as meaningfully diagnostic,
not just a total-time proxy — that reading is this entry's own extension.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** **Population:** native (USSR) and
foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires
over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF
p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport. The correlations described are all
between running-based specialized-developmental/competitive exercises — this entry does
NOT cover strength or jump-exercise transfer, which is markedly weaker (see
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] and
[[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]]). Applying these specific
coefficients to football skill-position speed training is Inference: football speed
development sits inside a team-sport context with far less training-time devoted purely
to sprinting than a specialized Soviet track program, so the magnitude of these
correlations should not be assumed to hold as-is.

**Example** — **Inference:** a 200m runner's training program built heavily around 150m
and 300m repeats at race-adjacent intensity is well-supported by this data (150m-to-200m
and 300m-to-200m correlations ran 0.707-0.888 / 0.724-0.842), slightly more so than a
program relying mainly on much shorter (30m) flying segments (0.708-0.730) for that
specific event — a small gap, not a large one.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification these
correlated exercises fall into. [[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] —
the much weaker transfer picture for non-running assistance exercises in the same event
group.

# Among Assistance Exercises, Multi-Jump Work (Ten-Fold Jump, Leg-to-Leg Bounds) Transfers to Sprinting Most Consistently — More Than Single Jumps, Throws, or Barbell Lifts

**What it is** — Comparing all the specialized-preparatory assistance exercises tested
against sprint/hurdle competitive results (barbell snatch, half squat, standing long jump,
vertical jump, triple jump from place, 10-fold jump from place, leg-to-leg jumps for 50m,
forward/backward shot throws), Bondarchuk identifies the **10-fold jump from place** and
**leg-to-leg (bounding) jumps for 50m** as "more transferable than other specialized-
preparatory exercises," measured not by having the single highest correlation coefficient
but by the number of qualification-level bands across which a positive cumulative effect
appears (PDF p. 99, printed p. 82). Concretely: leg-to-leg jumps for 50m showed a
cumulative effect on **all levels** for both men's and women's 100m, and across the full
range for women's 100m hurdles (12.80-15.80s) and men's 400m hurdles (49.50-55.50s) (PDF
p. 100, printed p. 83). **Exceptions to that consistency**, cutting against reading it as
uniform: leg-to-leg 50m appeared on only one qualification level in men's 200m (20.50-
21.00sec), men's 110m hurdles (15.50-16.00sec), and women's 400m hurdles (58.00-59.00sec)
(PDF p. 100, printed p. 83). By contrast, the standing long jump, vertical jump, and
triple jump from place did not show a uniform two-to-three-of-five-levels pattern: the
vertical jump appeared on five of five levels in men's 110m hurdles and four of five in
women's 100m hurdles, while the triple jump from place appeared on four of five levels in
women's 100m (PDF pp. 90-91, printed pp. 73-74) — stronger than "two-to-three for most
events" in those specific cases, even while the overall claim (multi-jump work is more
consistent than single jumps) still holds directionally. There is no high-jump or
pole-vault exercise tested against sprint results anywhere in this table set (Table 51's
rows are snatch, half squat, standing long jump, vertical jump, triple jump from place,
10-fold jump from place, leg-to-leg jumps for 50m, and forward/backward shot throws, PDF
p. 91, printed p. 74) — an earlier draft of this entry invented a high jump/pole vault
comparison that does not exist in the source; it has been removed. He generalizes: "with
an increase in a number of take-offs when executing the above mentioned jump exercises,
there is an increase in the number of cases of positive transfer" — proposing multi-jump
exercises "executed over long segments of time" (20-150m) as the most broadly transferable
jump category for track and field generally. (PDF pp. 100-101, printed pp. 83-84.) He adds
a practical recommendation this entry had not previously captured: specialists should
systematically use lightened and more complex (weighted) jump conditions for the full
duration of the sports-form cycle rather than sporadically as was then common, and should
attend to the optimal angle of incline used for speed vs. strength development, since
incline affects both effectiveness and the number of technical errors (PDF p. 101, printed
p. 84).

**Why it works** — His own stated mechanism: multi-jump exercises over distance "repeat
the biomechanical parameters of the competitive movement" more closely than single jumps,
"have a similar appearance to the muscle work regimes, and use the same intensity zones,"
and can duplicate the sprint's actual duration/segment structure (e.g. matching a starting-
acceleration segment specifically). (PDF p. 101, printed p. 84.) **Inference:** reading
this through [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], repeated bounding over a real
sprint-relevant distance sits closer to specialized-developmental than a single standing
jump does, which under [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] would predict
exactly
the stronger, more level-consistent transfer observed here.

**When to apply** — When choosing between plyometric/jump exercise variants for a
sprint-focused program, this data favors prioritizing repeated multi-jump/bounding work
over set distances (matched to the target phase of the sprint — acceleration vs. max
velocity) over single-effort jumps (standing long jump, vertical jump) as the more
consistently transferable choice, while still using single jumps for their own
diagnostic/training value.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** **A positive interrelationship begins
at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); Table 51's leg-to-leg values (0.406-0.561) all clear
that threshold. **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of
mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus
published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not
football, not team sport. "Leg-to-leg jumps for 50m" and "10-fold jump from place" are
specific, defined tests in this text, not a stand-in for every modern bounding or
plyometric variation. The claim is about *transfer consistency across qualification
levels*, not about which exercise has the single highest correlation value — do not
conflate the two when citing this entry. Applying this preference (multi-jump over
single-jump assistance work) to football speed/power training is Inference; no outside
plyometrics source was checked in this ingest to confirm the pattern holds beyond
Bondarchuk's own track and field dataset.

**Example** — **Inference:** a sprint-development block choosing between a session of
standing long jumps and a session of 10-15 continuous alternate-leg bounds over 30-50m
would, per this data, expect the bounding session to transfer more reliably across a wider
range of athlete ability levels.

**Related** — [[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]] — the
running-based exercises that transfer even more strongly than jumps in this event group.
[[claim--jump-event-exercise-transfer-patterns]] — the parallel (and partly consistent)
finding for jump-event athletes' own competitive results.

conflate the two when citing this entry. Applying this preference (multi-jump over
single-jump assistance work) to football speed/power training is Inference; no outside
plyometrics source was checked in this ingest to confirm the pattern holds beyond
Bondarchuk's own track and field dataset.

**Example** — **Inference:** a sprint-development block choosing between a session of
standing long jumps and a session of 10-15 continuous alternate-leg bounds over 30-50m
would, per this data, expect the bounding session to transfer more reliably across a wider
range of athlete ability levels.

**Related** — [[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]] — the
running-based exercises that transfer even more strongly than jumps in this event group.
[[claim--jump-event-exercise-transfer-patterns]] — the parallel (and partly consistent)
finding for jump-event athletes' own competitive results.

=== PDF 088
 
For development of speed-strength abilities in the training of different level athletes, a 
large number of strength, jump, and throw exercises are used.  Their portion of the total 
amount of training time, in relation to the tasks being resolved, the qualifications of the 
athlete and their individual characteristics, can comprise from 10-30% of the total sports 
form development cycle time.  The strength exercises are executed with and without the 
barbell, in addition to using various training devices.  The strength exercises, in 
comparison to others, produce a wider range of effects in the process of developing 
speed-strength abilities.  With their use, it is possible to selectively develop the muscle 
strength abilities such as speed, strength and “explosiveness”.     
 
In experimental research, two strength exercises have been studied---the barbell snatch 
and the half squat with the barbell on the shoulders. These exercises are most frequently 
used in the training of athletes having various sports qualifications.  They make it 
possible to evaluate the total level of development of strength abilities of all the body 
links of the athlete (barbell snatch) and strength of the leg extensors (half squat with 
barbell on shoulders).  
 
Besides this, these two exercises, according to their biomechanical characteristics 
(direction of movement, consecutiveness of including muscle groups in the work, 
regimes of muscle work, and so on) duplicate many strength exercises that are 
systematically used in the training process.  Knowing the results in each of these 
exercises makes it possible to predict achievement in other exercises and consequently, 
have a more complete picture of the transfer of physical abilities when using similar 
exercises.   
 
The data received testify to the poor interrelationship between the competitive event and 
the snatch and the squat with the barbell on the shoulders.  We will begin with the 100m 
run (tables 51, 56).  With the men, the cumulative effect in these two exercises was seen 
up to the level of 11.10 - 11.40 seconds.  With the women, in the snatch, it showed up 
71 
=== PDF 089
only on one level - 12.70-12.790 sec., and in the half squat with the barbell on the 
shoulders, on two levels (11.80-12.0 and 12.70-12.90 seconds).   
 
In the men’s and women’s 200m run, a positive interrelationship between the snatch and 
the competitive event was not observed on all levels of sports mastery.  What is pertinent 
to this is that in the half squat with the barbell on the shoulders, there is a cumulative 
effect which appears in the men on the level of 23.00-23.50 seconds and in the women, 
25.00-25.50 seconds (tables 52, 57). 
 
In men and women specializing in the 400m run, there is no correlational 
interrelationship between results in the snatch and the competitive event on all levels of 
sports mastery.  In the half squat with the barbell on the shoulders it is observed on the 
51.00-52.00 seconds level in the men and in the women, 55.00-56.00 seconds (tables 53, 
58).   
 
Somewhat different results are seen in the correlational analyses in the men’s 110m 
hurdle run and in the women’s 100m hurdles (tables 54, 59).  In men, the cumulative 
effect in the snatch is lacking only on two levels of sports mastery---16.00-16.60 seconds 
and 15.00-15.50 seconds.  In women, in the snatch a positive influence is not seen on all 
levels of sports mastery.  In the half squat with the barbell on the shoulders the 
cumulative training effect in men appears on the 14.50-15.00 seconds level and in the 
women - only on the 13.30-13.80 seconds level.  
 
In the 400m hurdle run, a positive interrelationship between the two strength exercises 
and the competitive event was not seen (table 55, 60).  Coefficients of correlation varied 
from 0.196-0.320.   
 
According to direction of movement, throws of the shot forward and backward have a 
consecutive inclusion of the basic body links that are close to that of the snatch exercise.  
They are similar to the power clean.  However, there is a difference between them in the 
muscle work regimes.  When using the throws of the shot forward and backward not only 
72 
=== PDF 090
is speed-strength developed, but also explosive abilities.  If in the snatch, in most track 
and field sprint and hurdle events a cumulative effect is noted on some level of sports 
mastery, aside from the 400m hurdles, then the throws of the shot forward and backward 
have a place only with 110m hurdlers on two levels--13.50-14.00 seconds and 14.00-
14.50 seconds.  In the other events it is absent, both with the men and women (see tables 
51-60). 
 
Greater transfer is seen in the standing long jump (see tables 51-60).  Results in the long 
jump, vertical jump and triple jump from place, make it possible to judge the speed-
strength and explosive abilities of the leg muscles that play a role during the starts, 
starting acceleration and run over the distance.  In almost all track and field sprint and 
hurdle events, there is a positive correlational interrelationship.   
 
Absence of the cumulative training effect was seen only in the women’s 400m run (see 
tables 51-60).  The training effect was seen most frequently in the 100m, 110 and 100m 
hurdle runners.  In men 100m runners, a positive relationship was found on two levels of 
sports results---11.10-11.40 sec. and 11.40-11.70 sec. In the long jump from place it was 
seen in women on the same comparative levels ---12.10-12.40 sec. and 12.40-12.70 sec.   
 
In the 200m run, the cumulative effect of this exercise to the competitive exercise in men 
was seen on the level of 22.50-23.00sec. and in the women 25.00-25.50sec.  It had a 
place on two levels in the 110m hurdle run ---14.00-14.50sec. and 16.00-16.50sec. and in 
the 100m hurdles, 13.0-13.80 sec. and 14.30-14.80sec. 
 
In the vertical jump a positive transfer of physical abilities in the men’s 100 meters was 
seen on three levels --- 10.80-11.10sec, 11.10-11.40sec, and 11.40-11.70sec, while in the 
women on two levels --- 12.10-12.40sec, and 12.40-12.70 sec.  In the 200m run it had a 
place only with the women---24.50-25.0sec and 25.00-25.50sec. In the men it was absent 
on all levels.  In the 110m hurdles the cumulative effect appeared on five levels of sports 
mastery while in the women 100m hurdlers on four levels.  In the 400m and in the 400m 
hurdles there was no positive interrelationship with the men as well as with the women.

Now we will look more closely at the results of the correlational analyses which revealed 
the essence of the positive interrelationship between the competitive events and the ten-
fold jump from place and the leg to leg jumps for 50m.  First it should be noted that these 
two exercises appear more transferable than other specialized-preparatory exercises 
(barbell clean, half squat with the barbell on the shoulders, throwing the shot put forward 
and backward, long jump from place, triple jump and vertical jump).  Here we don’t have 
in view higher coefficients of correlation but the number of cases of positive 
interrelationships which appear on different levels of sports mastery in each of the track 
and field sprint and hurdle events (see tables 51-60).   
 
Thus in the ten-fold jump from place, on the fifth level of sports results, the cumulative 
training effect appears in the men’s 110m hurdle run, ---from 13.50-14.0 sec to 15.50-
16.00 sec. and in the women’s 100m hurdle run, --- from 12.80-13.3sec to 15.3-15.8sec.  
82 
=== PDF 100
It had a role in the men’s 100m run in four instances from 10.50-10.80sec to 11.0-
11.70sec and in the women’s 100m,--- from 11.50-11.80sec to 12.40-12.70sec.   
 
The same held true in the women’s 200m run, --- from 23.50-24.00sec to 25.00-25.50sec 
and in the men’s 400m hurdle run, --- from 49.50-50.50sec to 52.50-53.50sec as well as 
in the women’s, from 54.00-55.00sec to 58.00-59.00sec.  The positive transfer was 
observed in the men’s 200m on three levels of sports mastery --- 21.50-22.00sec, 22.50-
23.00sec and 23.00-23.50sec and on two levels in the men’s 400m, --- 49.00-50.00sec 
and 50.00-51.00sec and in the women’s 400m, 52.00-53.00sec and 54.00-55.00sec. 
 
In the jumps from leg to leg for 50m, the cumulative effect appeared on all levels with the 
men as well as with the women in the 100m run.  In regard to the 200m run with the men 
it was not observed except on one level (20.50-21.00sec), and with the women, it had a 
place only on the 25.50sec to 12.70sec level. In the men’s 400m, a positive transfer took 
place on four levels (from 46.00-47.00sec to 49.00-50.00sec) and with the women, on 
five levels (from 50.00-51.00sec to 54.00-55.00sec).  In all cases there was a cumulative 
training effect in the women’s 100m hurdles (from 12.80-15.80sec) and in the men’s 
400m hurdles (from 49.50-55.50sec).  In the men’s 110m hurdles the cumulative effect 
was seen only on one level (15.50-16.00sec).  The same occurred in the women’s 400m 
hurdles (58.00-59.00sec). 
 
With an increase in a number of take-offs when executing the above mentioned jump 
exercises, there is an increase in the number of cases of positive transfer of physical 
abilities on different levels of sports mastery. This makes it possible to propose that of all 
the jump exercises found in sports practice (and there are several dozens of these) the 
most transferable to the competitive movement are those that are executed over long 
segments of time.  Related to this are the different jumps from leg to leg, multiple jumps, 
skips on one leg, double leg jumps and others, for distances ranging from 20-30 to 100-
150m. 
 
83 
=== PDF 101
The transfer ability of these exercises can be explained by the fact that they, to a good 
extent, repeat the biomechanical parameters of the competitive movement, have a similar 
appearance to the muscle work regimes, and use the same intensity zones.  The duration 
of the effect can correspond to the entire distance or its main joint parts (as for example 
the starting acceleration), and if necessary, the effect can be made greater.  Besides this, 
all of these exercises can be executed in lighter as well as in more complex (with weights, 
jumps or skips for height and other) conditions.   
 
Since the problem of using of lighter and more complex conditions when executing jump 
exercises has been touched upon, it should be noted that there is a straight line 
relationship to the specialized-developmental and competitive exercises.  They have been 
and are used at the present time by athletes of various sports qualifications. 
 
Without expanding this problem we propose that with time, the volume of jump exercises 
with the use of lightened and more complex conditions will significantly increase in 
comparison to the amount of work which is presently being done.  Of course specialists 
will have to resolve several problems.  First will be to show the optimal correlation 
between training loads executed in the standard, lightened and more complex conditions.  
Second will be to determine the weight to be used.  Third will be to not use lighter and 
more complex conditions sporadically as is presently being done, but systematically for 
the duration of the entire cycle of developing sports form.  Only in this way will it be 
possible to resolve the problem of developing speed (lightened conditions) and strength 
(more complex conditions) abilities.   
 
Specialists should also devote  attention to the selection of the optimal angles of incline 
of the roads used for development of speed or strength capabilities.  Dependent upon this 
is not only the effectiveness of developing the necessary physical abilities, but also the 
number of technical errors that appear. These errors always play a role when doing the 
exercises. 
 
84 
=== PDF 102
The absence of the cumulative training effect from the snatch and half squat with the 
barbell on the shoulders to the competitive event in the men’s and women’s 400m 
hurdles, as well as the barbell snatch to the 200 and 400m can be interpreted in different 
ways.  In one case, it indicates the ineffectiveness of the given exercise, while in another, 
that the positive transfer is conditioned by the use of other methodological means.  This 
relates primarily to the number of repetitions in one set, the compactness of the strength 
training sessions or their parts, and likewise the zones of intensity used.   
 
It is obvious that the cumulative effect from strength exercises will appear only when 
they are close to the competitive event according to the biomechanical aspects and 
methodological parameters.

In the triple jump from place, a cumulative effect was seen on four levels of sports 
mastery in 100m women runners---11.50-11.80 sec. to 12.40-12.70 sec.  With the men, 
the cumulative effect was seen in 110m hurdle runners---from 13.50-14.00sec to 15.00-
15.50 sec.  In the men’s 100m, there was a positive transfer on three levels of sports 
mastery---10.80-11.10sec, 11.10-11.40sec and 11.40-11.70sec.  In the women’s 200m 
there was a positive transfer on two levels of sports mastery,--- 24.50-25.00 sec and 
25.00-25.50 sec and in the 100m hurdles, 13.30-13.80sec and 14.30-14.80sec.  In the

50.00-51.00 sec. With the men and women in the 400m hurdles, it corresponded to 54.50-
55.50sec. and 56-57.00sec.

# The Barbell Snatch and Half Squat Transfer to Sprinting Only Up to a Narrow, Specific Performance Band, Then Stop

**What it is** — Tables 51-60 (PDF pp. 91-99, printed pp. 74-82) correlate the barbell
snatch and half squat (with barbell on shoulders) against 100m/200m/400m and hurdle
results across five to six performance bands per event. Bondarchuk's own reading: overall
interrelationship is poor, and where a positive ("cumulative") effect exists at all, it is
confined to specific, narrow bands rather than holding across all qualification levels.
Examples with locators: men's 100m snatch/squat "cumulative effect" only up to
11.10-11.40s (Table 51: snatch coefficients range from -0.186 at 10.20-10.50s up to only
0.396 at 11.10-11.40s); women's snatch shows an effect on only one band, 12.70-12.79s
(Table 56); in the 400m hurdles, "a positive interrelationship... was not seen" at all,
with correlation coefficients ranging only 0.196-0.320 (Table 55 itself at PDF p. 95,
printed p. 78; the "not seen" summary sentence and the 0.196-0.320 range are Bondarchuk's
own text at PDF p. 89, printed p. 72). **Exception:** men's 110m hurdles is not a narrow
band like the others — the snatch's cumulative effect there is "lacking only on two levels
of sports mastery" (16.00-16.60sec and 15.00-15.50sec), i.e. present on most levels (PDF
p. 89, printed p. 72). Throws of the shot forward/backward
were even weaker transfer exercises, positive only for 110m hurdlers at two narrow bands
(13.50-14.00s and 14.00-14.50s) and absent elsewhere. (PDF pp. 88-90, printed pp. 71-73.)
**A positive interrelationship begins at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59).

**Why he chose these two lifts.** Bondarchuk explains why the snatch and half squat were
the strength exercises studied, not an arbitrary pair: they let him evaluate total-body
strength (snatch) and leg-extensor strength (half squat) separately, and "according to
their biomechanical characteristics (direction of movement, consecutiveness of including
muscle groups in the work, regimes of muscle work, and so on) duplicate many strength
exercises that are systematically used in the training process. Knowing the results in
each of these exercises makes it possible to predict achievement in other exercises" (PDF
p. 88, printed p. 71). **Inference:** this entry's own caution — that the poor-transfer
finding "should not be assumed to hold for a different strength exercise variation without
its own data" — follows from that same passage but is this entry's extension, not a
limitation the author states himself; the author frames the two lifts as broadly
representative, not narrow.

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk gives both readings, not one: "the absence of the
cumulative training effect from the snatch and half squat with the barbell on the
shoulders to the competitive event in the men's and women's 400m hurdles, as well as the
barbell snatch to the 200 and 400m can be interpreted in different ways. In one case, it
indicates the ineffectiveness of the given exercise, while in another, that the positive
transfer is conditioned by the use of other methodological means. This relates primarily
to the number of repetitions in one set, the compactness of the strength training sessions
or their parts, and likewise the zones of intensity used." He closes with a general rule:
"the cumulative effect from strength exercises will appear only when they are close to the
competitive event according to the biomechanical aspects and methodological parameters"
(PDF p. 102, printed p. 85). **Inference:** in the terms this book itself defines, the
snatch and squat are specialized-preparatory exercises (per
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]]), sharing muscle groups with sprinting but
not its movement structure, velocity, or ground-contact regime — this classification-based
reading is this entry's own, not spelled out by the author in this passage.

**When to apply** — Use as historical caution against assuming barbell strength numbers
(snatch, squat) will keep predicting sprint improvement once an athlete passes a certain
performance level; per this data, once an athlete is already fast, further improvement in
these lifts stops tracking with further sprint improvement. This does not mean drop the
lifts (see [[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] for
Bondarchuk's own prescription on that point) — it means stop expecting them to be the
driver of further sprint gains at that point.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** **Population:** native (USSR) and
foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires
over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF
p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport; tested with a specific barbell snatch
and a half-squat-with-barbell-on-shoulders (not a full back squat, front squat, or
trap-bar variant). **Inference:** the finding should not be assumed to hold for a
different strength exercise variation without its own data, though the author himself
frames the snatch and half squat as broadly representative of systematically-used strength
exercises (PDF p. 88, printed p. 71), not as narrow or unusual choices. This is track and
field data; extending "barbell strength work plateaus in its transfer to top-end speed
past a certain level" to football speed training is Inference. No outside source was
checked in this ingest to confirm whether this pattern holds beyond Bondarchuk's own
dataset; treat it as this book's finding only until cross-checked.

**Example** — **Inference:** a high-level 100m sprinter already running 10.2-10.4s should
not expect squat or snatch PRs to reliably predict further 100m improvement, per this
data; a developing sprinter in the 11.0-11.5s range is more likely to still be inside the
band where this book's data shows a measurable (if still modest) positive relationship.

**Related** — [[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]] — the much
stronger transfer picture for running-based assistance work in the same event group.
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] — Bondarchuk's own
prescription for what to do once an exercise stops producing further transfer.

# Three Types of Training Transfer, Plus "Indifferent" (Double-Effect) Transfer

**What it is** — Bondarchuk names three types of training transfer (PDF p. 31, printed
p. 14):
- **Positive**: an increase in one exercise's result parallels an increase in another.
- **Negative**: an increase in preparation for one exercise coincides with a decrease in
  another.
- **Neutral**: no measurable effect either way.

He then adds a fourth term, drawn from outside literature, not presented as his own
addition: "In the specialized literature it is also possible to find 'indifferent'
transfer." He returns to it separately: "In addition to these three noted forms of
training transfer we more rarely meet with indifferent transfer" — **indifferent transfer
is the double-effect case**, not a synonym for neutral. It shows up "especially... when
training high level athletes who use a whole complex of different exercises," and can have
"a double effect on one another": a positive effect on one dimension and a negative effect
on another at the same time. Example: heavier-implement throws can be "positive... on
increasing the functional capabilities of the body systems and a negative effect on the
technique," and "there is a noticeable worsening of technique in some throws with the use
of heavier implements" (refs [18, 152]) — with increased strength, "a negative change in
the process of executing separate elements as well as the entire movement as a whole"
[152]. (PDF p. 31, printed p. 14.)

Bondarchuk gives a specific worked example: race walkers doing high volumes of aerobic/
anaerobic running in general preparation showed improved heart-circulatory/respiratory
function but worsened walking technique [94] — a positive-physiological/negative-technical
double effect. He also gives a remedy: walkers can avoid the negative influence "by using
mainly specialized-developmental and competitive exercises"; in other running events,
hurdles, and throws, coaches can select among exercises so "there would be more good ones
rather than poor ones," which "makes it possible to eliminate the negative influence on
technique in several weekly cycles." (PDF p. 32, printed p. 15.)

**Why it works** — For the three-way split, Bondarchuk gives no mechanism; he presents it
as received terminology. For the double-effect (indifferent) case specifically, he does
give an explanation: "The double effect of certain exercises on others (indifferent
transfer) is most frequently explained by the use of exercises which, from the beginning,
interfere with the unity between form and content" (PDF pp. 31-32, printed pp. 14-15) — the
same form-and-content framing used against the holistics' block method (see
[[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]). **Note on scope:** Chapter 1's
earlier discussion of E.L. Thorndike's "theory of identical elements" (PDF p. 20, printed
p. 3; see [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]) is presented by Bondarchuk
as the basis for the *specifist* position on transfer generally, not explicitly linked by
him to this positive/negative/neutral/indifferent typology — this entry does not claim
that link was Bondarchuk's own.

**When to apply** — Use the four-way split as a checklist when introducing a new exercise:
is the expected effect positive, negative, neutral, or a **double effect (indifferent)**
where it will help one quality while hurting another (most often physical capacity up,
technique down, from overloaded implements/loads)? The walking example is the clean
illustration. **Inference:** flagging any high-volume general-conditioning block for a
technical, timing-sensitive sport skill (sprinting, throwing, agility) as a double-effect
risk is this entry's own extension of the walking case, not something the passage states
for those sports; the author's own remedy (favor specialized-developmental/competitive
exercises, or bias exercise selection toward "good" over "poor" options) applies whichever
sport is in question.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** The category examples given (heavier
implements degrading throw technique, aerobic-volume race walkers losing walking
technique) are drawn from Soviet-era track and field research cited only by bracketed
reference number [18, 94, 152], not verified against the original sources in this ingest.
**Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification,
data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results
(PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport.
Extending "double effect" reasoning to football (e.g., heavy sled work degrading sprint
mechanics) is Inference, plausible by analogy but not something this passage tests.

**Example** — **Inference:** a college lineman doing high-volume heavy sled pushes for
GPP strength may show a positive effect on force production and a negative (double)
effect on start technique and shin angle if the sled load or volume is not periodically
reduced back toward the competitive movement pattern, echoing the walker's aerobic-volume
example here.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining,
staging) — **Inference:** a plausible mechanism this claim's negative-transfer cases could
run through (mismatch on one of the ten specificity dimensions), not a link the source
itself draws.

the process of executing separate elements as well as the entire movement as a whole"
[152]. (PDF p. 31, printed p. 14.)

Bondarchuk gives a specific worked example: race walkers doing high volumes of aerobic/
anaerobic running in general preparation showed improved heart-circulatory/respiratory
function but worsened walking technique [94] — a positive-physiological/negative-technical
double effect. He also gives a remedy: walkers can avoid the negative influence "by using
mainly specialized-developmental and competitive exercises"; in other running events,
hurdles, and throws, coaches can select among exercises so "there would be more good ones
rather than poor ones," which "makes it possible to eliminate the negative influence on
technique in several weekly cycles." (PDF p. 32, printed p. 15.)

**Why it works** — For the three-way split, Bondarchuk gives no mechanism; he presents it
as received terminology. For the double-effect (indifferent) case specifically, he does
give an explanation: "The double effect of certain exercises on others (indifferent
transfer) is most frequently explained by the use of exercises which, from the beginning,
interfere with the unity between form and content" (PDF pp. 31-32, printed pp. 14-15) — the
same form-and-content framing used against the holistics' block method (see
[[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]). **Note on scope:** Chapter 1's
earlier discussion of E.L. Thorndike's "theory of identical elements" (PDF p. 20, printed
p. 3; see [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]) is presented by Bondarchuk
as the basis for the *specifist* position on transfer generally, not explicitly linked by
him to this positive/negative/neutral/indifferent typology — this entry does not claim
that link was Bondarchuk's own.

is the expected effect positive, negative, neutral, or a **double effect (indifferent)**
where it will help one quality while hurting another (most often physical capacity up,
technique down, from overloaded implements/loads)? The walking example is the clean
illustration. **Inference:** flagging any high-volume general-conditioning block for a
technical, timing-sensitive sport skill (sprinting, throwing, agility) as a double-effect
risk is this entry's own extension of the walking case, not something the passage states
for those sports; the author's own remedy (favor specialized-developmental/competitive
exercises, or bias exercise selection toward "good" over "poor" options) applies whichever
sport is in question.

implements degrading throw technique, aerobic-volume race walkers losing walking
technique) are drawn from Soviet-era track and field research cited only by bracketed
reference number [18, 94, 152], not verified against the original sources in this ingest.
**Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification,
data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results
(PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport.

mechanics) is Inference, plausible by analogy but not something this passage tests.

GPP strength may show a positive effect on force production and a negative (double)
effect on start technique and shin angle if the sled load or volume is not periodically
reduced back toward the competitive movement pattern, echoing the walker's aerobic-volume
example here.

staging) — **Inference:** a plausible mechanism this claim's negative-transfer cases could
run through (mismatch on one of the ten specificity dimensions), not a link the source
itself draws.
=== PDF 031
Types of Training Transfer 
 
There are three types of training transfer: positive, negative, and neutral.  In the 
specialized literature it is also possible to find “indifferent” transfer. 
 
Positive transfer of training means that there is a positive effect of one exercise on 
another.  In other words, with an increase in the sports result in one exercise, a parallel 
increase takes place in another exercise. 
 
In negative transfer of training there is always a negative interaction between the 
exercises being used.  Here, with increased preparation in one exercise, there is a 
simultaneous decrease in other exercises. 
 
In neutral transfer of training there is no increase or decrease in sports achievement.  The 
training does not show any affect on another training. 
 
In addition to these three noted forms of training transfer we more rarely meet with 
indifferent transfer.  This is especially so when training high level athletes who use a 
whole complex of different exercises, and depends on their coordination structure and 
strength of their influence.  At the present time, the interrelationships between the 
exercises are complex and unpredictable, and they may have a double effect on one 
another. For example, there may be a positive affect on increasing the functional 
capabilities of the body systems and a negative effect on the technique an exercise [92].  
In track and field, there is a noticeable worsening of technique in some throws with the 
use of heavier implements [18, 152]. In these cases, with an increase in strength, there is 
a negative change in the process of executing separate elements as well the entire 
movement as a whole [152]. 
 
The double effect of certain exercises on others (indifferent transfer) is most frequently 
explained by the use of exercises which, from the beginning, interfere with the unity 
between form and content.  Examples of indifferent transfer can be in the systems of

here is the use of a high volume of aerobic and anaerobic running for long periods of

# Throwing Lighter and Heavier Versions of the Same Implement Transfers to the Competitive Throw Almost Universally, Across Nearly Every Level of Mastery

**What it is** — Tables 69-84 (PDF pp. 116-130, printed pp. 99-113) correlate results
throwing lighter/heavier implement weights (e.g., a 5-10kg shot, a 1.5-2.5kg discus, a
0.5-1kg javelin, a 3-16kg hammer/weight) against the competitive-weight throw, for men and
women across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer. Bondarchuk's summary quote is broader
in scope than "lighter/heavier vs. competitive": "there is almost always a place for
mutually correlated interrelationships between special-developmental exercises (throws and
'shot putting' various implements having different weights from place) and exercises with
lighter, heavier and competitive implements" (PDF p. 132, printed p. 115) — i.e. it covers
standing throws of various weights against full lighter/heavier/competitive throws, not
only the lighter/heavier-vs.-competitive pairing this entry's title highlights. He gives
**three** exceptions, not two: javelin, no relationship between the 0.6kg implement and
the 3-4kg standing throw; javelin, no relationship between the 0.7kg and 4kg implements;
and, in women, "no cumulative effect at the 40-45m level in throws with the competitive
implement and in standing throws with the shot weighing 3kg" (PDF p. 132, printed p. 115).

**The dose that produces the strongest correlations.** "The greatest amounts of
correlational interrelationships were most frequently found in cases where the deviations
[from competition weight] was insignificant in relation to the competitive — from 10-20%."
The weakest values in the whole dataset came from the largest deviations: 0.425 for the
16kg hammer weight at the 60-65m level, and 0.365 between the 5.0kg and 7.260kg shot at
the 20-21m level — notably, that 0.365 weak value sits at the *top* competitive level, not
a low one, so "near-universal transfer" should carry that qualifier. (PDF p. 115, printed
p. 98.) **A positive interrelationship begins at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); the
0.365 value above only barely clears it.

He illustrates the practical power of this with individual elite-athlete case data
(**single-case, untested**, not aggregate correlation): two-time Olympic hammer champion
Yu. Sedikh held unofficial world-best-adjacent marks in the 5, 6, 8, 9, and 10kg
implements and the 16kg weight alongside his 86.74m competitive record, with year-by-year
dynamics (1980-86) showing his lighter/heavier implement results moving in lockstep with
his competitive result in 35 of 38 tracked instances (PDF p. 142, printed p. 125, not PDF
pp. 130-131 as an earlier draft of this entry cited). The same passage contrasts this with
his *specialized-preparatory* exercise results, which tracked the competitive result in
only 8 of 35 cases and were "autonomous" (untracking) in the other 27 — a sharp difference
from the implement-weight throws' near-lockstep pattern (PDF p. 142, printed p. 125).
Discus thrower R. Ubartasa's five-year log similarly shows his implement-weight throws
increasing alongside his competitive result in 29 of 34 instances (Table 88, PDF p. 141,
printed p. 124), against his specialized-preparatory exercises tracking in only 32 of 49
instances (32 with, 17 without) (PDF p. 141, printed p. 124) — the same implement-weight-
vs.-specialized-preparatory contrast Sedikh's data shows.

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: lighter/heavier-implement throws are
"identical to themselves according to the basic parameters beginning with the technical
and rhythmical composition and ending with the consecutiveness of inclusion of the
muscular groups... the muscle work regimes and so on" (PDF p. 115, printed p. 98).
**Inference:** in the terms of [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], this is as
close to a pure specialized-developmental exercise as exists in this book (the same
movement, only the resistance changes), which under
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] would predict the near-universal
positive transfer observed — this classification-based reading is this entry's own, not
stated by the author in these terms.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this reads as the strongest, most consistent transfer
finding in the excerpted chapters — for throwing events specifically, varying implement
weight while keeping the competitive movement intact is a reliably transferable training
method across nearly the full range of athlete qualification, more consistent than any
strength, jump, or sprint assistance exercise tested elsewhere in this chapter — but that
cross-chapter comparison is this entry's own judgment, not a claim the author makes; his
own claim is narrower: "throws with lighter and heavier implements appear to be the most
transferable to the competitive exercise" (PDF p. 115, printed p. 98), without comparing
across chapters. He does flag a real caveat: heavier implements can degrade technique
(release angle, trunk lean, reduced amplitude), an effect he says clears up "in several
weekly cycles" once the heavier implement is dropped — the double-effect pattern named in
[[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]].

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported for the aggregate correlational
finding (Tables 69-84)**, but the Sedikh/Ubartasa individual case data (Tables 85-88) is
**untested**: single elite-athlete case studies, presented as illustration, not as
independent evidence of the mechanism, and Bondarchuk himself frames them as examples
rather than proof. **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of
mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus
published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not
football, not team sport (the case-study athletes are elite Soviet-bloc Olympic/world
champions specifically). This finding is specific to implements that can be made lighter
or heavier while keeping the throwing motion otherwise intact (shot, discus, javelin,
hammer); there is no directly equivalent implement-weight manipulation in most football
skills, so applying "vary the resistance, keep the movement identical" as a general
training principle to football (e.g., weighted-ball throwing for a quarterback) is
Inference by analogy, not something this data tests.

**Example** — **Inference:** a hammer thrower's training plan built around a rotation of
5-6 different implement weights (lighter and heavier than competition weight, ideally
within the 10-20% band shown to correlate most strongly) targeting both speed and strength
qualities within the same movement pattern is strongly supported by this data as a
transfer-reliable method, more so than substituting generic barbell strength work for
that same purpose (see [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]).

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification
explaining this exercise's near-maximal transfer. [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]
— the much more limited transfer picture for barbell strength exercises in the same event
group. [[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]] — the double-effect pattern behind the
heavier-implement technique caveat. [[heuristic--implement-weight-dosing-and-throwing-boom-warning]]
— the historical dosing/volume data (10-20% deviation band, the "throwing boom" overdose
case) this entry's correlational finding does not itself cover.
