# Barbell Snatch, Power Clean, Squat, and Bench Press All Transfer to Throwing — But Only Up to a Specific Result Level, Then Plateau

**What it is** — Across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer, Bondarchuk finds that all
four major strength exercises (snatch, power clean, squat with barbell on shoulders,
bench press — bench excluded for hammer throwers, who "do not use it") show a positive
transfer to the competitive throw **in most event/sex groups** (exception: javelin, see
below), but **only up to a specific result level for each exercise and event**, after
which the correlation with further competitive improvement disappears. Worked examples
with locators: in discus, snatch transfer ended at 45-50m (men) / 55-60m (women); power
clean and squat ended at 50-55m; bench press extended furthest, to 55-60m (men) / 65-70m
(women). In hammer, snatch ended at 60-65m, power clean 65-70m, squat 60-65m; women's
cumulative effect ran further, to 45-60m across all three. In shot put, snatch ended at
17-18m (men)/15-16m (women), power clean at 14-15m (men)/14-25m (women — a probable typo
in the printed text, not an OCR artifact: the source PDF has a real text layer, not a
scanned/OCR'd page, so this is either a source misprint or an unusually wide band), squat
at 19-20m (men)/17-18m (women), bench at 18-19m (men)/19-20m (women). **In javelin, the
"all four transfer" pattern breaks**: snatch and power clean both ended at 65-70m (men);
at the 50-55m level "there was no correlation seen" for either the squat or the bench
press (men); women's snatch ended at 60-65m, power clean 50-55m, bench 45-50m, and squat
"showed no cumulative transfer effect" at all. (PDF pp. 133-135, printed pp. 116-118.)
Bondarchuk's own aggregate summary across the whole book, at the close of this chapter:
"specialized-preparatory exercises have a positive influence on an increase in the sports
result in the basic event but up to a specific level of sports mastery. Further on, they
do not show a positive effect." (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158.) He also notes, from the same
chapter's closing material, that "the leading throwers (world and Olympic champions and
world record holders) do not always have the best absolute results in the specialized-
preparatory exercises" (PDF p. 139, printed p. 122) — a further data point supporting the
ceiling: being the best thrower does not require the best strength numbers.

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for why the ceiling occurs at these specific
levels; **Inference:** this is consistent with a training-age/diminishing-returns pattern
common across strength and power sports — general strength qualities predict performance
strongly at lower levels of mastery, but as an athlete's absolute strength approaches the
level "required" for the skill, further strength gains stop being the limiting factor and
technical/specialized qualities (captured better by the specialized-developmental
exercises in [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]) take over as the
binding constraint. Bondarchuk does not state this diminishing-returns interpretation
himself in the excerpted text; it is this entry's own reading.

**When to apply** — Use as a rationale for shifting a throwing (or other power-sport)
athlete's programming emphasis away from general barbell strength work and toward
specialized-developmental work (implement-weight variation, technical throws) once the
athlete's **competitive result** crosses into the "cumulative effect ends here" distance
band for their event (the ceilings above are competition-distance bands, not strength-load
thresholds), rather than continuing to chase strength PRs as the primary lever for
competitive improvement.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** These are group-level ceilings; the
author explicitly cautions against reading them as fixed for every individual: "if we take
into consideration individual and not group indices in the above mentioned strength
exercises, then it is very possible that in individual cases we will see the cumulative
effect appearing on different levels of sports mastery for each athlete. They will be very
individualized. It may show that in women it can be even higher than in men" (PDF p. 135,
printed p. 118). **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of
mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus
published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not
football, not team sport; using a specific set of four lifts (Olympic-style snatch and
power clean, not necessarily modern variations; a barbell squat and bench press without
stated depth/technique standards). The exact result-level thresholds are specific to this
1970s-80s dataset and should not be treated as current standards. This entry does NOT mean
"stop lifting" once the ceiling is reached — see
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] for the author's own
explicit statement that these exercises should still be used at reduced volume for
maintenance and restoration. Applying this ceiling-effect logic to a football strength
athlete (e.g., an offensive lineman) is Inference: no football population data exists
here, and a lineman's "competitive exercise" is far less discrete than a single measured
throw.

**Example** — **Inference:** a discus thrower already throwing past 50-55m, per this
data, should not expect further squat PRs alone to keep driving discus distance; continued
improvement is better targeted through implement-weight variation and technical work (see
[[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]), with strength work maintained
rather than chased — though per the individualisation caveat above, some individual
athletes may see the ceiling at a different distance than the group figure.

**Related** — [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]] — the
specialized-developmental alternative that keeps transferring past this ceiling.
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] — what to do with
strength work once this ceiling is reached, in the author's own words.
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] — the parallel (and even more limited)
ceiling pattern for strength exercises in sprinting.
=== PDF 134
and in women, 55-60m.  In the power clean and in the barbell squat, a positive 
interrelationship ended at the level of 50-55m.  In the bench press, with the men the 
cumulative effect was seen on the 55-60m level and in the women, 65-70m.   
 
In hammer throwers, a positive interrelationship between results in the throws of the 
competitive implement and the snatch was observed on the level of 60-65m, with the 
power clean at the 65-70m level and with the barbell squat, at the 60-65m level.  In 
women, the cumulative training effect was fixed between the above mentioned exercises 
at the level of 45-60m.   
 
A positive transfer in the shot put with results in the barbell snatch were seen on the level 
of 17-18m, but with the power clean at 14-15m, in the squat with the barbell on the 
shoulders at 19-20m and in the bench press, 18-19m.  In women, transfer of the 
cumulative effect to the competitive event was fixed in the barbell snatch at the level of 
15-16m, in the power clean at 14-25m, in the squat with the barbell on the shoulders at 
17-18m, and in the bench press, 19-20m. 
 
In the javelin throw, a positive interrelationship was seen between indices in the 
competitive event and in the snatch and power clean on the level of 65-70m.  At the 50-
55m level there was no correlation seen in the squat with the barbell on the shoulders and 
in the bench press.  In the women, a positive transfer to the competitive event was seen 
with results in the barbell snatch on the level of 60-65m, in the power clean up to 50-
55m, and in the bench press, up to 45-50m.  There was no cumulative transfer effect with 
the barbell squat. 
 
The compiled data is evidence of the fact that the transfer of physical abilities with 
strength exercises to the competitive event is seen up to the determined level of sports 
results.  In this, the results in some strength exercises are somewhat higher than in others.  
Thus, the indices in the barbell snatch serve to achieve higher results in the main event in 
the shot put (men), in the hammer throw (men and women) in the discus throw and 
javelin (women).  In the power clean, the cumulative effect was even greater in the discus

throw and in the hammer throw (men and women).  Indices in the barbell squat have 
greater transfer to the shot put, hammer and discus (men and women).  In the bench 
press, the transfer is seen for a long time in the shotput and discus throw (men and 
women).   
 
If we take into consideration individual and not group indices in the above mentioned 
strength exercises, then it is very possible that in individual cases we will see the 
cumulative effect appearing on different levels of sports mastery for each athlete.  They 
will be very individualized.  It may show that in women it can be even higher than in 
men.  This is fully explainable since the level of strength indices in women, according to 
sexual indicators, are significantly lower than in men.   
 
Some of the biomechanical characteristics (as for example consecutiveness of including 
body links in the work being done), and likewise the muscle work regimes, of throws of 
the shot forward and backward are also seen in the barbell snatch and to a certain extent, 
in the power clean.  Besides this, in the process of executing these exercises all body 
links of the throwers participate in the work being done.  However, ignoring the 
coordinational similarity between the above mentioned exercises, results of the 
correlational analysis show that the cumulative effect of the throwing exercises to the 
competitive event in all throw events is seen only on the lower levels of sports 
achievements.   
 
Thus in the discus throw, results in the throw of the shot forward do not serve to increase 
results in the competitive event on all levels of sports mastery.  In women, the cumulative 
effect is seen only on the level of 40-45m.  In throws of the shot backward, a positive 
transfer has a place both with the men as well as with the women.  In men, it is seen up to 
the level of 45-50m and in the women up to 50-55m. 
 
In the men’s hammer throw, results in the throws of the shot forward that served in the 
transfer of the cumulative effect was seen up to the level of 55-60m, and in the women it 
was absent.  What is pertinent to the positive correlational interrelationship between 
118 
=== PDF 139
training of women, the cumulative effect was observed on all levels of sports 
mastery in five of the nine exercises. 
 
 
4. In the training of javelin throwers, most transfer is seen from the barbell snatch, 
power clean, standing long jump and triple jump.  The cumulative effect had a 
place at the 65-70m level.  In training of the women, four exercises had a positive 
transfer ending at the level of 40-45m and in two cases, on the 45-50 and 55-60m 
levels.  Most transfer appears in the barbell snatch and in the 30m run from a low 
start.  A positive training transfer in these exercises has a place at the level of 55-
60m. 
 
In conclusion, we will note that in the theory and practice of track and field throws, there 
is sufficient experimental material to substantiate that the leading throwers (world and 
Olympic champions and world record holders) do not always have the best absolute 
results in the specialized-preparatory exercises. The absolute best achievements are 
considered those which were shown by the athletes over the duration of several past 
decades.  Most frequently these indices were of athletes during one or another Olympic 
cycle moving into the world elite.  In addition, former or present world record holders in 
the throws of the competitive implement always appear as unofficial world record 
holders, or they show results close to them, in the throws of lighter and heavier 
implements, as well as in specialized-developmental exercises (see tables 85, 87).

collection method is also stated directly: "The data used was received mainly through the
use of questionnaires from native and foreign athletes having different sports
qualifications. The questionnaires were carried out over the course of four Olympic
cycles. Also analyzed were tests results of individual athletes as recorded in different
literature sources." (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59.) Table 8 lists non-Soviet athletes by name
(L. Evans, T. Smith, M. Cox, and Bulgarian athletes; PDF p. 48, printed p. 31). Every
entry's "When NOT to apply" section in this folder now states population as: "native
(USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from
questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8,
printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport." Per the brief's
rule for Soviet-era/single-lab findings, everything ingested from this book is capped at
`supported`, and dropped to `untested` for the author's own single, unverified theoretical
proposals (e.g. individual case-study illustrations, the A-B-C tie-in-effect example) or
set to `contested` where the source states a finding two different ways and both are kept
visible (e.g. the aerobic/anaerobic-alactate time-to-form direction, PDF pp. 165, 173).
Nothing in the excerpted chapters rises to `proven` in this batch: even where a concept
(e.g. positive/negative/neutral transfer) echoes a name Bondarchuk himself cites from
outside his own study (Thorndike), no outside source was independently checked in this
ingest, so every entry stays capped `supported` or lower and says explicitly, in its own
words, when a broader claim is this entry's own reading rather than something either
Bondarchuk or a checked citation states.

Also add: a positive correlation in this book's tables is defined as **r >= 0.349** (0.423
for women's pole vault specifically), and the correlational data throughout is scoped to
training systems **without steroid use** — the preface states steroid use raises results
in all exercises used and not used, masking which exercise actually drove the transfer
(PDF pp. 8-9, printed pp. vii-viii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59; PDF p. 111, printed p. 94).

Every reported correlation coefficient in this book is presented **without sample sizes,
significance tests, or population age/sex breakdowns beyond "high qualification" vs "low
qualification"** groups (the tables' own note: "the coefficient of correlation of high
level athletes is in the numerator and for low level athletes, in the denominator," with
the numerator/denominator convention flipped without warning between the sprint tables
(41-50, high/low) and the throws tables (70, 72, 74, 76, 78: "low qualifications... in the

and `claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal.md` for the locators. Treat
any single number pulled from these tables with that reversal risk in mind.

**The population throughout is native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of mixed
qualification** (sprinters, hurdlers, jumpers, throwers, middle/long/ultra-distance
runners, race walkers), data collected mainly through questionnaires "from native and
foreign athletes having different sports qualifications" over four Olympic cycles, plus
published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59). An
earlier draft of this file said the population was "entirely within the USSR system" —
that was wrong; see the correction above. **Nothing here is football, team-sport, or
non-track-and-field population data.** Any application to football or other team sports

`staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/`.

**Method.** I dumped the text layer of every page of `Transfer of Trainng in Sports - Bondarchuk.pdf`
with PyMuPDF (0-based index, the same as the entries) and read every page cited below myself,
including all pages the fixer says it did not re-dump. I rendered PDF 218-219 as images (the
reference list). Locators are written "PDF n / p. X" (0-based; viewer = n+1; printed = n-17 in the body).
Cross-cutting checks (em dashes, population line, 0.349, "Soviet", [[links]]) were run by script over
all 21 files, not taken from the log.

## Read this first: what the fix log says was done but was not

1. **The new heuristic puts a paraphrase in quotation marks.** `heuristic--implement-weight-dosing-and-throwing-boom-warning.md`
   says the throwing boom "produced negative after-effects" in quotes. PDF 133 / p. 116 does not
   contain that phrase. Its actual words: specialists recommend raising SDE volume "up to reasonable
   amounts in order to avoid the errors made by throwers in past years" and "There should be an
   optimal amount everywhere or the after-effect will be fraught with negative consequences."
   The phrase came from round 1's Missing Item 4 paraphrase and was then quoted as source text.
2. **The aerobic entry's `contested` reason quotes the wrong PDF 164 sentence** and leaves out
   PDF 172 (details in its row). The rewrite now overclaims in the opposite direction ("the author
   states the opposite").
3. **The log says 0.349 was added "to every Chapter 2 claim entry ... that cites correlation
   coefficients." It is absent** from `claim--endurance-event-transfer-range-widens-with-distance.md`
   and `claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect.md` (both cite coefficients or correlation bands).
4. **"Soviet" population wording is still there** in `claim--model-characteristic-tables-exist-by-qualification.md`
   ("1970s-80s Soviet track and field data", "Soviet-era numbers"), `claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations.md`
   ("a specialized Soviet track program") and the new heuristic ("Soviet-bloc throws training";
   PDF 133 names no bloc). Table 8, the very table the model-characteristics entry describes,
   lists L. Evans, T. Smith, D. Carr, M. Cox and Bulgarian athletes (PDF 48 / p. 31).
5. **Body em dashes were not touched anywhere.** The script count excludes the house-style
   "**What it is** —" headers and still finds em dashes in the body of every file: aerobic 10,
   endurance 8, jump-event 10, model-char 7, sprint-hurdle 8, sprint-jump 7, sprint-strength 7,

   tests 4, three-viewpoints 5, transfer-factors 7, tie-in 6, stage-duration 8, implement-dosing 11,
   maintain 6, conjugated 4, `_book.md` 10. **Titles with em dashes** (not covered by the header
   exception): aerobic, sprint-jump, throws-strength, maintain, `_book.md`.
6. **Process narration inside entry bodies.** "corrected from a NO-GO review finding", "The prior
   version of this entry...", "an earlier draft of this entry...", "new entry, review's Missing Item 4"
   appear in current-vs-distant, transfer-factors, aerobic, jump-event, sprint-jump, model-char,
   throws-implement and the new heuristic. That history belongs in the fix log. A vault reader
   should see only the corrected content.

**The next fix pass should check its work with grep, not by trusting the fix log.**

- Every [[link]] resolves.

- The steroid-free scope is stated with PDF 9 in the tie-in entry and `_book.md`.
- All three `_book.md` corrections from round 1 were applied.
